News.title: Dog killed after car set alight in McDonald’s car park as man, 28, arrested – as cops hunt 2 men who tried to rescue pet
News.content:
FATAL FIRE Dog killed after car set alight in McDonald’s car park as man, 28, arrested – as cops hunt 2 men who tried to rescue pet

A DOG died after a car was set on fire in a McDonald’s car park as cops investigate the shocking blaze.

Firefighters were called to put out the burning vehicle in the fast food chain’s car park at around 12.15am on Monday, June 22.



Tragically, a dog was found dead inside the vehicle at the food outlet on Winchester Road, Petersfield.

Officers have launched an investigation to establish exactly what happened and how the fire started.



A 28-year-old man of no fixed address was arrested on suspicion of arson and causing unnecessary suffering to an animal.

He was also arrested on suspicion of driving otherwise than in accordance with a licence and having no insurance.

The man has since been bailed with conditions until September 22 while enquiries continue.

Officers have now been reviewing CCTV footage as part of their investigation.

They are particularly keen to speak to two men who were seen in the area around the time of the fire.



The pair appear to have tried to get into the vehicle in an attempt to help the dog.

Cops believe they could have important information about what happened and are urging them to come forward.

The spokesperson said they “appreciate that these are not the clearest images”, but urged anybody with information to get in touch, quoting reference number 44260294619.”

More to follow… For the latest news on this story keep checking back at The Sun Online

News.title: Teen, 18, sexually assaulted by masked man in park as cops launch urgent hunt
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

SEX ATTACK Teen, 18, sexually assaulted by masked man in park as cops launch urgent hunt

A YOUNG woman was allegedly sexually assaulted in park by a masked man.

Officers were called to the scene in Scholes, West Yorkshire on Wednesday evening to reports of an attack on the 18-year-old victim.

The suspect is described as wearing a balaclava, as well as a black jacket top and trousers.

Police are appealing for witnesses to come forward as enquiries continue – with the alleged incident taking place at 9.30pm off Old Popplewell Lane.





West Yorkshire Police said: “The 18-year-old woman is being supported by specially trained officers.

“The suspect is described as a white man, in his 20s, slim build. He was wearing a balaclava, black jacket black top and black joggers.

“Enquiries are ongoing by Kirklees District Safeguarding team.

“Anyone with information or who saw a man matching this description in the area is asked to contact police via the Live Chat options on our website at www.westyorkshire.police.uk/livechat quoting reference 13260446481

“Information can always be given anonymously via Crimestoppers on 0800 555 111.”

News.title: The five desperate plots cornered Putin is hatching as Ukraine brings war home & why tyrant will fight to dying breath
News.content:
AS Ukraine brings the war to Russia’s doorstep with devastating strikes, desperate Vladimir Putin is hatching plots to take back momentum.

The tyrant has suffered months of crippling blows to his war machine as Ukraine unleashes an endgame blitz on oil hubs and logistics warehouses.



In a bid to put an end to the snowballing success, Putin – who will fight to his dying breath, according to Ukraine’s former foreign minister – could unleash one of five options to seize back the upper hand.

The cornered dictator has been forced to come up with new ways to win the war because of Ukraine’s long-range drone and missile attacks, experts told The Sun.



Major e-commerce platform Wildberries, dubbed Russia’s Amazon, as well as oil refineries and transport links have all suffered massive attacks at the hands of Kyiv’s 40-day onslaught.

Ex-foreign minister Dmytro Kuleba told The Sun the Kremlin despot has several final-resort options up his sleeve.

Describing Putin’s diminishing options, Kuleba said the tyrant may look to create a “new weapon” to better defend Russia against Ukrainian drones.

He said: “He can generate a technological breakthrough where he comes up with a new weapon or with a solution to intercept Ukrainian drones and missiles.”

Putin’s second plan could be “a tactical solution”, Kuleba said.

He explained: “Finding a way to use the current Russian army in a better way, in a more efficient way than it is being used now.”



He added: “The third one is mobilisation in Russia… sending more cannon fodder to the front line and dominating through mass, not through effectiveness.”

Putin’s fourth plot could be further expansion of Russian sabotage and interference with the rest of Europe.

Kuleba suggested the Russian leader could “expand the theatre of war by provoking Nato with limited military operations”.



And in a chilling warning, Kuleba said Putin could continue the threat of a nuclear strike to put an end to Kyiv’s winning streak.

“Putin will be playing with the first four options one way or another while threatening the fifth option,” he said.

Kuleba also warned: “Putin will be fighting wars until his last breath.”

The Russian president’s refusal to recognise Ukraine as a legitimate state is an obsession that will last for the rest of his life, he added.

Ex-Brit Army officer Hamish de Bretton-Gordon said mass mobilisation could backfire.



He said it could be “Putin’s final throw of the dice, and [it] may well actually not work at all”.

Volodymyr Zelensky warned last month the tyrant could force 500,000 conscripts into his army to gain the upper hand on the frontline.

De Bretton-Gordon said: “As soon as the middle classes in Moscow and St. Petersburg are sending their sons off to the front, then that is a very different situation.



“If there’s mass mobilisation… the wealthy in St. Petersburg and Moscow will not allow their children to go to the front line to be slaughtered [like] one-and-a-half million others.”

Russia analyst Natia Seskuria said Kyiv’s relentless pressure means Putin could expand his shadow war on Nato.

She said: “I think it is a likely scenario that Russia will try to escalate its asymmetric warfare against the European allies.”

Seskuria noted that mass mobilisation is “always” on the cards for Putin – but said it could be “a very risky move”.

Highlighting the success of the 40-day operation, she added: “Putin’s options are narrowing, and that is probably one of the most important consequences of Ukraine’s pressure campaign.”



Meanwhile, Russia expert Emily Ferris pointed to air defences and tech as key weaknesses Putin may look to address.

“When it comes to the technology, I think Russia are behind… it will take time for them to catch up and eventually they probably will,” she told The Sun.

Ukraine’s devastating blitzes on key infrastructure had forced resources away from the battlefield, she added.



“They’ve had to divert resources from the frontline to the rear, so they have to now invest a huge amount in protecting oil refineries,” Ferris said.

Kuleba also detailed key steps for Ukraine to win the war – adding that the combination of all of them would guarantee success.

He said: “Of course, long-range strikes and middle-range strikes conducted by Ukraine are a very important part of that package.

“They cannot change anything on their own, they are inflicting enormous damage on Russia, but other elements should also complement these efforts.

He called for more sanctions to be slapped on the Putin regime, which should be “comprehensive and enforced”.



“Political pressure, so Putin does not feel that there are big players who are willing to support him, should be increased,” he said.

“The economic situation in Russia should continue to deteriorate, and the frontline should be brought to a stalemate, it should be immobile.”

Ukraine’s endgame blitz has brought the momentum of Putin’s invasion to a standstill.

Kuleba explained how Kyiv has been able to put their foot on Russia’s neck over the last few months.

He said: “It’s an outcome of a group of complex factors. Long-range bring war into Russia and distract Russia’s attention.



“Mid-range strikes knock out Russian logistics on the frontline, weakening the frontline positions. Heavy deployment of drones to the frontline by Ukraine limits the advance of Russian forces.

“And Ukrainian resilience deep at home against continued missile and drone strikes defy Putin’s ambition to break Ukraine down from the inside.”

He added: “There is also an important issue of communications on the frontline, where the disconnection of Russian units in Ukraine from Starlink significantly complicates their operations.”

Emphasising the impact of the 40-day operation, Seskuria said: “Ukraine has managed to successfully deconstruct Putin’s key narrative that the ‘special military operation’ has been taking place distant from Russian households.”

She expects Kyiv’s drone attacks to continue, adding: “This should be understood as the closing of the initial phase of Ukraine’s deep-strike campaign, not the end of the broader strategy.”



De Bretton-Gordon said the strikes have “brought this war virtually into every sitting room in Russia, where most people, particularly the middle class, the elite who run the country, have been pretty much untouched by the war”.

He added: “Almost nowhere in Russia is safe from Ukrainian attack.”

And the ex-Army officer suggested Putin’s power is under threat.

“Putin’s position is actually now becoming in the balance and in peril,” he said. “And many people are suggesting that it’s time for a new Russian leader.”

While Ukraine’s efforts have taken a toll, Ferris warned that the long-term impact on Russia’s war machine remains to be seen.



She noted that the strikes had “highlighted how weak the rear defences are in Russia”.

She said: “Russia assumed that anything beyond the frontline behind Russia proper was pretty much immune from attack.

“Over the past 18 months, that’s proven not to be the case because of the development long-range missiles and drones, things which Russia has been much slower to catch up with.”

While Kyiv hopes its strike campaign will force Putin to the negotiating table, Kuleba doubts the Russian leader can be persuaded to scale back his ambitions.

“He is not seeking negotiations and he does not believe that Europe has the agency to negotiate,” Kuleba said.



The minister said Putin only views the US as an equal counterpart worth negotiating with.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Over the last two years, Donald Trump has repeatedly tried to broker peace between Putin and Zelensky.

But with diplomatic talks stalled indefinitely, the burden may fall entirely on Ukraine to ensure the momentum remains in its favour.

News.title: Desperate hunt for missing woman last seen ‘entering sea alone’ at popular UK beach as huge search operation launched
News.content:
FRANTIC SEARCH Desperate hunt for missing woman last seen ‘entering sea alone’ at popular UK beach as huge search operation launched

A MAJOR search is under way for a missing woman last seen entering the sea alone at a popular UK beach.

The huge search operation was launched after she was seen getting in the water from Weymouth Esplanade, Dorest, shortly after 11pm yesterday.

Cops are growing increasingly concerned for her welfare and have appealed to anyone who may have seen her to come forward.

Officers have been carrying out searches in the area with support from a National Police Air Service helicopter, HM Coastguard and the RNLI.





The woman is described as being of average build with long hair.

She was wearing a long, flowing dress when she entered the water, which was a lighter colour at the top.

Police said the woman was alone at the time of the incident and is not believed to have returned.

No belongings have been found during a search of the beach area.



Inspector Mark Latter, of Dorset Police, is urging any witnesses to get in touch.

He said: “We are growing increasingly concerned for the woman’s welfare and are carrying out enquiries to locate her.

“The woman was on her own at the time of the incident and no belongings have been found following a search of the beach area.

“I am appealing to anyone who may have witnessed a woman matching the description in the Weymouth Esplanade area at the time of the incident to contact us.



“I am also directly appealing to the woman to get in touch with us if she has left the water and is safe and well.”

Anyone with information is asked to contact Dorset Police by calling 999, quoting incident number 8-598.

News.title: Child, 4, drowns in beach bar pool while parents swim in the sea as couple arrested at Brit holiday hotspot
News.content:
POOL TRAGEDY Child, 4, drowns in beach bar pool while parents swim in the sea as couple arrested at Brit holiday hotspot

A FOUR-year-old boy has drowned in a beach bar swimming pool in Greece.

The child’s parents – who were taking a dip in the sea on the Greek holiday island of Paros when the tragedy unfolded – have been arrested.



The bar owner, who is the establishment’s registered lifeguard, has also been detained.

Cops said two young women noticed the boy was unconscious in the pool and quickly raised the alarm.



A bar employee dived in and pulled the boy out, before paramedics rushed to the scene.

Efforts were made to resuscitate the child, but he tragically died.



A probe has been launched into his death.

Police are understood to be questioning the bar owner and boy’s parents as part of a preliminary investigation.

It comes after Spain was hit with a spate of child drownings earlier in the summer.

Six children died in the space of just 72 hours in June and sparked an urgent warning for tourists with kids.



Sebastián Quintana, an expert in drowning prevention, lambasted a “tragic lack of supervision” and warned holidaymakers to keep an eye on their kids at beaches and in pools.

In almost all of the cases, the parents were absent when their child drowned.

Quintana warned: “The lack of attention, supervision, or even absence at the bathing area by the adults in charge is the main cause of these human tragedies.

“A child won’t scream for help. Drowning is a very quick and silent event.”

One of the victim’s was tragic Eleri Ellesmere, 3, who drowned while on holiday with her parents in Majorca.



Desperate family members battled to save her at Villa Francisca before she was rushed to hospital.

But she could not be saved and was declared dead the following day.

Paying tribute, Eleri’s heartbroken mum Cerys said: “What should have been an idyllic family holiday has turned into every parent’s worst nightmare. A nightmare we cannot wake up from.

“Our precious little Eleri Fairy was involved in an accident during the holiday.

“Unfortunately, despite unbelievable effort and attempts to heal our little girl made by us and the Palma health services, we were left with her on life sustaining support.



“Me and Joe were with her every single second and our little girl showed incomprehensible strength to try and stay with us. This was not enough.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Less than a month after the series of deaths, a six-year-old Belgian boy drowned while on a family holiday in Barcelona.

Witnesses said there was no lifeguard on duty at the swimming pool, which was 5m deep at points.

News.title: Fresh foreign aid farce as £13m of taxpayers’ cash helps Mozambique sell gas while Brit families face soaring bills
News.content:
MORE than £13million in UK taxpayer cash is helping Mozambique profit from flogging ­natural gas.

It comes despite new drilling being banned in the North Sea, stopping Britain from getting similar returns.



The Foreign Office has funnelled money to the East African state to help it better collect revenues and manage finances.

The project was set up in 2018 to ensure Mozambique state can “reap the imminent benefits of gas revenues”.



The UK gets no return on its investment.

The £13.2million Tax and Economic Governance Programme runs until at least the end of 2026.



It could instead fund annual energy bills of nearly 9,000 struggling British families or restore £300 Winter Fuel Payments for 44,000 pensioners.

Mozambique is soon set to rake in around £4.6billion a year from selling gas and taxes on firms operating in its territory.

Critics slammed the double standard and called for Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband to scrap the deal.

Reform’s Robert Jenrick said: “This is nuts. Reform will slash foreign aid and get drilling again in the North Sea.”



The Foreign Office said: “The Tax and Economic Governance programme helps prevent money-laundering and strengthens Mozambique’s ability to identify and remove funding that could be directed to terrorist groups, protecting the UK both at home and abroad.”

News.title: Man, 75, dead & woman rushed to hospital after fire rips through building as at least 3 others left needing treatment
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

FIRE TRAGEDY Man, 75, dead & woman rushed to hospital after fire rips through building as at least 3 others left needing treatment

A 75-YEAR-OLD man has died with a woman raced to hospital after a horror fire tore through a building.

At least three other people were treated for smoke inhalation at the scene after the blaze broke out at a property on Ridgway Road in Shelton, Stoke on Trent.

Emergency services, including an air ambulance, scrambled to the property where they found the elderly man dead.

The building was evacuated and fire crews eventually managed to extinguish the flames.





The force are working with Staffordshire Fire and Rescue Service to establish what started the fire.

Police added that the man’s next of kin have been informed and his family are being supported by specialist officers.

They are appealing for any witnesses to come forward.

A spokesperson for Staffordshire Police said: “A man has sadly died and four others suffered smoke inhalation following a fire in a property in Shelton.



“We were alerted to a fire by colleagues at Staffordshire Fire and Rescue Service in a property on Ridgway Road at around 12:50pm today.

“Fire crews extinguished the fire quickly and the building was evacuated.

“Sadly, a man aged 75 was found deceased and four others were treated for smoke inhalation, with one woman in her 60s being taken to hospital.

“The next of kin have been informed and are being supported by specially-trained officers.



“A scene has been set up whilst we work with fire investigators to determine how the fire started.

“Anyone with information about the fire should call 101 quoting incident 432 of 8 August.”

News.title: Strait of Hormuz could soon reopen as deal between Iran and Oman looms, US official claims
News.content:
THE Strait of Hormuz could soon reopen as a deal between Iran and Oman looms, a US official has claimed.

They said progress was made in talks between the nations, which sit on either side of the Strait.



A deal between Iran and Oman over control of the strategic ­waterway is seen as crucial to a wider peace agreement in the US’s five-month war with Iran.

The official, who did not want to be named, said: “There is progress between Oman and Iran, and we expect a deal soon.



“Once it is announced to restore commercial shipping without impediments, the United States will lift the blockade of Iranian ports.”

Before President Donald Trump and Israel launched the war on Iran, about one in five barrels of oil consumed worldwide went through the Strait.

But Iran has fired on ships that try to cross without permission.

Meanwhile, Lebanon and Israel have agreed on a shortlist of countries to ­verify the disarmament of terror group Hezbollah.

It is part of a US- brokered deal to end the war in Lebanon.

News.title: Andy Burnham to embark on cost of living tour through the UK
News.content:
The prime minister is set to announce "a series of measures to make life easier" for those struggling with the cost of living in the coming days, Downing Street says.

No 10 says Andy Burnham's plans are to "give people some room to breathe". He will also focus on ways of "improving high streets" as he embarks on a tour of the UK.

But the government is facing continued pressure over its early release scheme for prisoners in England and Wales â with criticism of the fact that two of PC Andrew Harper's killers will be eligible from next year.

Burnham is also likely to face pressure for more action on the cost of living â although significant interventions are unlikely before October's Budget.

Even then, Chancellor John Healey has made it clear he will oversee "strong fiscal discipline" â which will limit how much the government has to spend.

The prime minister has been on holiday this week, but Downing Street said he would be in "listening mode" in the coming days as he tours the UK's nations and regions and works on a "10-year plan to bring back hope".

A spokesman for the prime minister said: "He thinks Westminster has got used to telling people that everyday hassles â like hidden pricing and consumers being ripped off â must be accepted as part of life.

"He doesn't think that's right. That's why he's going to start rolling out a series of pro-consumer cost of living measures to give people some room to breathe."

The spokesman added: "He's also going to be kicking off his summer tour around the country, getting out of Westminster and meeting people where they are.

"The prime minister is going to be in listening mode to help inform his 10-year plan to bring back hope and make Britain better off."

There are, though, likely to be continued questions about the forthcoming early release scheme, due to start in October.

One of Burnham's first acts in Downing Street was to order a review which limited the range of people who would be eligible.

But those convicted of manslaughter will still qualify for the scheme â including two of the killers of PC Andrew Harper.

The prime minister has faced calls from PC Harper's family, former senior police officers and opposition politicians for them to be denied early release.

But he has said he cannot go any further without risking prison capacity. Downing Street said on Saturday night that position remained unchanged, despite reports the prime minister could revisit the case.

The Conservatives said the government's "tax hikes and red tape are hammering our high streets".

Shadow chancellor Mel Stride said: "This is breathtaking hypocrisy from Burnhamâ¦ they are forcing businesses to close, destroying jobs and driving up prices for the public.

"Meanwhile, Labour are plotting to release dangerous criminals onto our streets, leaving people feeling unsafe in their communities."

Liberal Democrat Treasury spokeswoman Daisy Cooper said struggling high street businesses "need more than a new PM embarking on a vanity tour this summer".

She said the PM should adopt the Lib Dem plan for high streets: "That means reversing the damaging jobs tax, delivering an emergency VAT cut for hospitality, replacing broken business rates and cracking down on the ghost landlords leaving our shop fronts vacant."

Reform UK's economic spokesman Robert Jenrick said: "If Andy Burnham wants to help people with the cost of living, he should scrap the green levies and taxes on energy bills and rule out tax rises at the Budget."

News.title: Fifa criticises campaign to oust president Infantino
News.content:
Fifa has strongly criticised what it calls a "concerted and ongoing effort" to "undermine" the organisation and its president Gianni Infantino.

The statement follows a Daily Telegraph report, external which claimed Infantino's alleged lover was given a severance payment by Uefa after he had an affair while he was its general secretary.

A Fifa spokesperson told the Telegraph Infantino "strongly denies" the allegations and that they are "categorically untrue".

Fifa has now itself hit out at "unsubstantiated assertions and demonstrably false claims", adding that "speculation and insinuation should not be presented as fact".

Infantino has come under increasing pressure from Uefa and European football associations over his aborted Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal.

FFE would have meant a new company being created to manage commercial and ticketing rights, with 21% sold off to a private investment company.

Uefa has said it has lost confidence in Infantino, while Norwegian Football Federation (NFF) president Lise Klaveness on Friday called on the Swiss-Italian to resign.

European football's governing body says its threat to boycott Fifa events remains on the table, adding that assurances the FFE plan could not be revived have not been received.

"The Fifa president was democratically elected by Fifa's Member Associations and continues to serve with their mandate," Fifa said in its statement on Saturday.

"It is increasingly evident that there is a concerted and ongoing effort by some to undermine Fifa and its president.

"Those who do not have the support of Fifa's member associations should not seek to achieve through allegation, insinuation or misinformation what they cannot achieve through Fifa's established democratic processes."

Opposition to Infantino is largely from within Europe.

The Mexican Football Federation broke ranks with its regional governing body Concacaf to come out in support of Infantino.

It echoed a statement from Conmebol - South America's governing body - in saying it would reject any attempt to remove Infantino without a vote involving all 211 Fifa member countries.

Infantino is also unanimously backed by the 54 nations of the Confederation of African Football (Caf).

News.title: Killed a month after his wedding - why PC Andrew Harper's death touched so many
News.content:
On the night of 15 August 2019, Lissie Harper got a knock at the door. She thought it was her husband Andrew coming home from work.

Instead, it was uniformed officers, there to tell her that the man she had married four weeks earlier had been killed while on police duty.

"Everything I had known in my life to be true was robbed away. Every ounce of beautiful peace, gone," Lissie later said of the moment she was told.

They had met as teenagers and were together for 13 years.

In her eulogy at his funeral, Lissie recalled how Andrew would pass her notes in class.

They were, she said, "true childhood sweethearts, loving one another more and more with each passing day".

They had been about to go on their honeymoon.

But, on that night nearly seven years ago, everything changed.

The case has been back in the headlines because two of PC Harper's killers â Albert Bowers and Jessie Cole â will become eligible to be released early under government plans to tackle prison overcrowding.

As the disturbing details of the case are revisited, his family, fellow officers and the public are outraged once more â at what happened, and at the perpetrators' impending release.

PC Harper's death was brutal and devastating, causing shock, anger and an outpouring of grief across the country.

Pictures of the smiling faces of his teenage killers laughing and joking as they left court only added to that anger.

PC Harper had been about to head home at the end of a long shift when he and a colleague were called to reports of a burglary.

He was "going beyond the call of duty", the prosecutor at the Old Bailey trial in 2020 said.

During the case, haunting dashcam footage from the police patrol car was played showing the moment PC Harper confronted teenagers Henry Long, Bowers and Cole down a dark country lane. He then disappeared from view.

His ankles had got caught in a strap trailing behind the car being driven by Long that had been used to tow a stolen quad bike.

PC Harper was dragged for over a mile. He died on the road. His police badge and stab vest were found scattered along the route.

The three teenagers were tried for murder. In the end, the jury convicted Bowers and Cole of manslaughter. Long had already pleaded guilty to that offence.

It meant the jury was not sure that PC Harper's killers knew they were dragging the officer behind the car.

But the Judge, Mr Justice Edis, described it as a manslaughter case which was "very close to a case of murder" in its seriousness.

News.title: Australia is the planet's extinction hotspot, but one animal offers a glimmer of hope
News.content:
"Eyes peeled," comes the order from the front passenger seat.

Obediently, we scan the ends and tops of logs, looking between low scrub and patches of vivid wildflowers for a flash of stripes or a dart of movement.

Eluding us is the numbat, a rare Australian marsupial which could be the love-child of a chipmunk and an anteater.

Numbats were once populous across the bottom half of the continent, but Dryandra Woodland â in the south-western corner of Australia â is one of the few places they remain.

As we slowly roll along bush tracks, researchers explain how this annual trip helps plot the species' survival.

Classified as endangered until this month, numbats have been bouncing back. This team's efforts have seen them scratched off the international red list of threatened species - a rare glimmer of hope in a country facing an extinction emergency.

This part of Australia is the front line of that crisis: a last stand for many species driven to the brink by feral pests, disease, urban development, habitat destruction and climate change.

Winging over our car at one point is the endangered Carnaby's cockatoo. On an island just off the coast is one of the last surviving pockets of the world's rarest marsupial, the Gilbert's potoroo. Diving in the sapphire waters around it is the increasingly scarce Australian sea lion.

News.title: Kellie Bright to leave EastEnders after 13 years
News.content:
EastEnders star Kellie Bright is to leave the soap after playing one of its key characters, Linda Carter, for 13 years.

She arrived in Albert Square with on-screen husband Mick, portrayed by Danny Dyer, when they became the new owners of the Queen Vic pub.

Carter's matriarch character has been central to major storylines including plots about murder, sexual assault and alcoholism.

Bright said she made the "tough decision" to leave more than a year ago but "happily" agreed to stay on to be part of an "exciting storyline".

The BBC has promised "unmissable drama" before her on-screen exit, which is said to be a "while away" yet.

Executive producer Ben Wadey described the actor as being "the beating heart of EastEnders" and said she had become "a classic EastEnders icon".

Viewers have seen the much-loved character at the heart of many emotional storylines including in 2014 when she was raped by her brother-in-law Dean Wicks.

More than 7m people watched the episode which prompted dozens of complaints. The sexual assualt led to long-running story arc about family conflict and trauma.

News.title: Zendaya saw me on the red carpet and her jaw dropped - I'm still in shock
News.content:
"I can't zip this! Mummm?"

This was 29-year-old Zainab Jiwa, calling out for help squeezing into a corset while filming a "get-ready-with-me" TikTok video. It's a scene many 20-somethings still living at home will relate to.

The difference is, Zainab was on her way to the recent London premiere of The Odyssey, one of the summer's biggest blockbusters.

She was invited there as a guest and says she caught the eye of Hollywood megastar Zendaya, thanks to her custom look: a striking gold gown complete with a hood.

"She just walked past, and she saw me there. Her jaw just dropped, so did mine," Zainab tells me.

"It was just a stare-off for a minute, and she was like, 'Oh my god, amazing, amazing,' and then she just walked off."

"Iâm still in shock,â she adds. âThe thought of her noticing my outfit blew my mind."

The interaction went viral, external with 19m TikTok views. Her phone blew up.

While Zendaya has been ruling the red carpets with high-fashion "method dressing" â where stars match outfits to a film's themes â Zainab is perhaps proving that independent creators like her can give Hollywood a run for its money.

Zainab, who is Muslim and wears a hijab, is also often one of the only people covering her hair at premieres, but she says finding ways to incorporate modest wear is part of the fun.

"Even though you're covered, you can still find a way to be on theme.â

News.title: How weight-loss medication is changing relationships with alcohol
News.content:
There is a growing body of research into the link between weight-loss drugs and alcohol consumption.

The drugs, with brands including Wegovy, Mounjaro and Ozempic, contain semaglutide or tirzepatide, which mimic a natural hormone called GLP-1. This suppresses appetite and keeps people feeling fuller for longer, helping them to lose weight.

Early research suggests that because these drugs affect the reward response in the brain, they can reduce cravings for substances including alcohol and nicotine, says Dr Christian Hendershot of the University of South Carolina.

He published a small-scale study, external in 2025 in which participants with alcohol use disorder craved alcohol less while taking Ozempic. Alcohol use disorder, sometimes referred to as alcoholism, is described by the NHS as drinking in a way that is harmful.

A study, external from the University of Colorado Anschutz published last week also suggested that GLP-1 medications in pill form led to fewer days of heavy drinking in people with mild to moderate alcohol use disorder.

People taking the drugs told BBC News that alcohol had affected them in different ways: some said their cravings for it had gone, drinking had made them feel nauseous or uncomfortably full, or they had got drunk more quickly. Others said they had not noticed any effect on their relationship with alcohol.

Before she started taking Wegovy, Lisa says she drank between six and eight bottles of wine a week with friends. But she had sometimes worried about whether this was too much and whether it could damage her health.

NHS guidance, external is that people should not drink more than 14 units a week on a regular basis, which is about six medium glasses of wine or six pints. Drinking too much in the long term can lead to liver damage, high blood pressure and increased risk of cancer.

Lisa says that since starting on the medication she has more than halved her consumption. At a recent day festival, she drank three glasses of wine over the course of nine hours. Previously, she would have had two bottles plus a couple of vodka mixers, she says.

Alcohol has always been a big part of her social life and when she stopped drinking for a few weeks in the late 2010s, she realised friends had stopped inviting her to social events. It led her to start drinking again.

This time round, Lisa says that she still looks forward to drinking wine, but after having a couple of glasses she simply cannot stomach any more.

"I still feel involved in things because I'm still drinking but drinking a lot less," Lisa says.

For years, Warren Thomas, 45, from Colchester, had enjoyed an occasional beer with his family after work, as well as one or two heavy drinking sessions with his friends each month.

But when he spoke to his friends on weight-loss medication about his plans to start taking Mounjaro, they warned him that it could affect how much he drank.

Warren says he noticed the effect within 24 hours of his first dose in mid-June. "I just don't want to drink," he says. "I've just got no appetite for it."

When he went out for his friend's birthday last month, he felt "light-headed and a little bit giddy" after two beers, he says.

"My tolerance level to drinking is now zero," he says.

There is no formal advice in the British National Formulary, a guide to dispensing medicine used by doctors and pharmacists, about whether people on weight-loss drugs should stop drinking alcohol, says Prof Russell Hearn, a GP and professor of medicine at King's College London.

But he gives careful advice to his patients. "Alcohol has a lot of calories in it and if your goal is to lose weight, drinking less will definitely help you with that alongside changing your diet while you're on a GLP-1," he says.

For people like Lisa and Warren, drinking less alcohol has been a happy bonus. But recent graduate Faye Goodwin, 20, feels that it has hampered her social life.

When Faye drinks she says she gets nauseous very quickly and sometimes throws up or gets bad acid reflux.

Faye, who got in touch with BBC Your Voice, has been taking Mounjaro since she was 18 and does not really know what it is like to drink alcohol without the impact of weight-loss medication. But she says she once took a month off the jabs and was able to drink without experiencing any nausea.

News.title: What it's like to chase solar eclipses around the world
News.content:
On Wednesday, parts of Europe will be plunged into daytime darkness as the moon passes in front of the sun, temporarily blocking its light and casting a shadow across the continent.

For many of us, it will be a once-in-a-lifetime experience. But for some, following eclipses has become something of an addiction.

Armed with two high-spec cameras, a specialist telescope and a drone, Mark Griffiths has spent two days driving from Cheshire to Galicia - one of the best places to view the eclipse - to record the event.

It's a hobby that started six years ago, when he went to Shetland to see the northern lights - though the weather was so dreary he "didn't see anything".

But it didn't put him off and he soon found he couldn't stop. He loved the thrill of witnessing and capturing the sky's most spectacular events.

News.title: Banksy works cost public almost £150,000
News.content:
Three artworks by street artist Banksy have cost taxpayers almost Â£150,000 in cleaning operations and security so far, with the bill expected to rise.

The largest single cost relates to a mural painted on the Royal Courts of Justice in September 2025, where removal efforts and security have so far cost more than Â£85,000.

The Ministry of Justice (MoJ) says it has spent Â£50,000 trying to remove paint from the wall of the Grade II-listed building in Carey Street. A further Â£35,300 was spent on overtime and security costs.

The spending was disclosed to the BBC through Freedom of Information requests and is likely to reignite debate over whether Banksy's work is vandalism or valuable public art.

News.title: Irish government jet travels to UAE for Kinahan extradition
News.content:
An Irish government jet has travelled to the United Arab Emirates (UAE) as part of an operation to extradite suspected crime boss Daniel Kinahan.

Kinahan was arrested in Dubai under a warrant issued by the Irish courts in April but has fought attempts to extradite him.

His appeals have been unsuccessful and it is expected that he is due to be flown back to Ireland on Sunday, according to Irish broadcaster RTÃ.

He will then be taken to the Special Criminal Court in Dublin.

On Kinhan's return to Ireland, RTÃ have said that a large security operation will be in place and the prison service has also upgraded facilities in the maximum-security Portlaoise Prison.

The US government imposed sanctions on him in April 2022 after he and other members of his family were identified as leaders of the Kinahan organised crime cartel.

Kinahan also had ties to the world of sport via his now defunct boxing management company MTK Global, which represented more than 100 boxers including Tyson Fury and Carl Frampton.

Irish authorities are expected to prosecute him for his involvement in leading an organised crime group.

An extradition agreement is in place between the UAE and Ireland and it was used to extradite Sean McGovern, a "senior lieutenant" in the organised crime group.

He was sentenced to 24 years in prison in June for directing the activities of a criminal organisation.

News.title: Simon Levy victims urged to come forward as police accused of 'litany of failures'
News.content:
Police have urged more victims of Simon Levy to come forward, as London's victims' commissioner said a "litany of failures" had allowed him to kill two women and rape a third.

Andrea Simon called for a review on the "failure to monitor him appropriately" when the 40-year-old was known to police as a sexual predator.

British Transport Police said women who recognised Levy as their attacker should report it, while the Met Police said it had investigated whether he had more victims, including further murders.

Meanwhile, the Independent Office of Police Conduct (IOPC) said a police constable is under investigation for gross misconduct, and a detective sergeant is facing a misconduct investigation.

On Friday, Levy was found guilty of murdering two women and raping a third in London while he was being monitored by the Met Police for being a convicted sex offender. He had previously committed a string of sex attacks.

The BBC reported how a series of grave failings by police, prosecutors and the courts left Levy free to murder, rape and sexually assault women.

Levy is due to be sentenced on Wednesday.

News.title: Charity watchdog investigates aid charity over alleged Hamas links
News.content:
A UK-based aid charity is being investigated by counter-terror police and the charity watchdog over alleged links to Hamas.

The Charity Commission launched an inquiry into Muslim faith-based charity Al-Khair Foundation on Friday.

Counter Terror Policing London (CTP) also confirmed investigations into the charity, with two search warrants on addresses in Croydon, South London.

The foundation said it is "co-operating fully" with the inquiry and had filed a serious incident report with the watchdog before it was launched.

A spokesperson for the foundation said: "Everywhere we work we are firmly committed to ensuring that the funds entrusted to us by our generous donors are used for their intended purpose: meeting the humanitarian needs of poor and marginalised people in the communities we serve.

"Al-Khair Foundation is deeply committed to supporting those in need in Gaza. Our significant support over many years has included providing food parcels, hot meals, clean water, medical aid, shelter materials, winter assistance and orphan and family support."

The Al-Khair Foundation provides emergency relief and developmental support in "some of the world's most impoverished areas", according to its website.

Hamas is designated as a terrorist organisation by the UK and US governments.

It comes after last week Mohammad Yousef Hasna, 45, from Istanbul, Turkey, was arrested in the UK over US accusations of conspiring to funnel money and supplies to Hamas through a "sham charity".

The US Department of Justice did not name the "sham charity" in their press release.

The Al-Khair foundation maintains that Hasna is not an employee but works with one of its global partners to enable the delivery of aid around the world.

Hasna is being held following his arrest by the UK's National Crime Agency (NCA) and pending extradition proceedings before he can be taken to New York to face the US charges.

The US Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York alleged Hasna used his senior role at a "purported global humanitarian organisation to coordinate directly with Hamas's senior leadership regarding the delivery of funds and supplies to Gaza, and the distribution of those funds and supplies at Hamas leadership's instructions".

Hasna is charged with conspiring to provide material support to Hamas, conspiring to finance terrorism and financing terrorism.

Each charge carries a maximum penalty of 20 years in prison, the US Department of Justice said.

US Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg said: "The money that flows from sham charities like the one described in the complaint fuels Hamas's terrorist activities, including the atrocities the group committed on October 7".

The Charity Commission said the Al-Khair Foundation recorded an income of more than Â£74m in the financial year ending 31 July 2025. The commission added it was made aware of the allegations against Hasna and "immediately started examining the serious concerns raised".

"The commission has now escalated its engagement to a statutory inquiry," the commission added.

Al-Khair is also subject to a legal order restricting some financial transactions being made without the consent of the Charity Commission.

News.title: Woman attacked by bed bugs during Travelodge stay
News.content:
Thirteen days after Hannah Stephenson stayed a night in a Travelodge hotel, she is still itching with red lumps over her body - a nightmare she would not wish on her "worst enemy".

The 31-year-old from Bassingbourn had been out with friends in Cambridge and decided to book a one-night stay at the hotel on Newmarket Road on 26 July to save money instead of getting a taxi home.

The next morning, she woke up to a "horrible realisation", feeling itchy with red lumps over her body and blood spots smeared on the bedding â the tell-tale signs of bed bugs, she said.

A Travelodge spokesperson said: "We are deeply sorry for Ms Stephenson's experience and how distressing an incident like this can be."

Stephenson said a lovely evening with friends had turned into a horrible morning.

"It was just a lovely wholesome time of Cambridge sightseeing and pubs, and now it is tarnished by these bedbug bites," she said.

"It wasn't until I saw the blood and the bugs that I realised what had happened."

News.title: Widdecombe police reopen investigation into incident at Farage's home, BBC understands
News.content:
Counter-terrorism police investigating the killing of Ann Widdecombe have reopened an inquiry into an incident at Nigel Farage's south London home, the BBC understands.

It is understood to relate to what the Reform UK leader described as a "lit incendiary device" being pushed through his letterbox in April 2025.

Counter Terrorism Policing (CTP) London said it was looking into an "attempted burglary" at a property as part of the Widdecombe murder investigation, but did not confirm the home was linked to Farage or why it might be connected to the killing of the former MP.

CTP London has also referred itself to the police watchdog over how the initial investigation into the Farage incident was handled.

Police said at the time that "damage was caused to a door but nothing was stolen".

Both CTP London and the Metropolitan Police were involved in enquiries. No arrests were made and the investigation was closed.

But on Friday, CTP London said a new line of inquiry had been identified that was not "pursued by them at the time".

The Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) said it had "decided to independently investigate the conduct of a Counter Terrorism Policing London staff member following a referral received earlier [on Friday]".

A statement continued: "The conduct relates to an allegation the individual failed to identify and pursue a line of enquiry relating to an attempted burglary reported in April 2025."

CTP London said it would "full engage" with the watchdog's investigation, adding: "The victims and families in both investigations have been updated today, and we continue to support them."

Ann Widdecombe, the 78-year-old former Conservative minister and Reform UK spokeswoman, was found dead at her home in Devon last month with serious injuries.

Joshua Kerry, from Rotherham in South Yorkshire, was later charged with her murder.

Kerry was initially arrested on suspicion of murder on 11 July, before being additionally arrested on 13 July on suspicion of the commission, preparation or instigation of acts of terrorism.

Widdecombe had served as Tory MP for Maidstone in Kent for 23 years and was appointed to ministerial roles in Sir John Major's government in the 1990s.

News.title: Strictly dancers Ola and James Jordan separate after 23 years of marriage
News.content:
Former Strictly Come Dancing stars James and Ola Jordan have confirmed they have separated after more than 20 years of marriage.

The former professional dancers were regulars on the show for several series after first featuring in 2006.

The couple in a statement said they were "taking some time apart as we work through very difficult personal challenges".

"This has been an incredibly painful and emotional journey for us both and it certainly wasn't an easy decision," they said in a joint post shared on their Instagram accounts.

The couple said James had moved out the family home some time ago and they "don't know exactly what the future holds".

"Right now, more than anything we ask for kindness, empathy and a little privacy as we work through this as a family."

The couple's manager Vickie White had prevously said in a statement: "It is with great sadness that I can confirm that James and Ola began a trial separation some time ago

"Their shared priority remains co-parenting their daughter, Ella, and they are committed to putting her wellbeing first.

"They would greatly appreciate your understanding as they navigate this difficult time."

Ola Jordan won the Open Polish Championship in 1999 when she was 17 years old and became James' dance partner shortly afterwards in March 2000.

She moved to England a month later and the pair got married in October 2003.

James appeared on Strictly from 2006 to 2013 while Ola appeared on the show until 2015.

Ola's celebrity partners included wildlife presenter Steve Backshall and Welsh sprinter Iwan Thomas, while James danced with former international gymnast and broadcaster Gabby Logan, as well as The One Show presenter Alex Jones.

News.title: Hundreds flying out of Birmingham Airport left without luggage
News.content:
She described seeing a "build up" of luggage at the airport, after problems with the luggage belt, but had been assured by staff that it would be loaded on to the plane.

But on arrival at Dalaman they were told by the pilot that no bags had been loaded.

"We have heard nothing about compensation, no communication when our luggage is expected, we've heard nothing about who is liable for it. Is it the airport? Is it TUI? Is it our travel insurance? Who are we meant to go to? We've had nothing from anybody", Chapman said.

"It's just radio silence from the airport, apart from literally telling people 'we've got an issue'".

The first day of their holiday was spent travelling to a shopping centre to buy essentials for "for the next few days" but she added "we have no idea how long this is going to last".

"There are families all over the world at the moment with nothing and no idea of what's going on," she said.

"It's really important that Birmingham Airport are held accountable, and sort this out."

News.title: Transfer news LIVE: Arsenal identify Vinicius Jr alternatives and Cristian Romero eyes shock switch
News.content:
Why Arsenal Want Bruno Guimaraes So Badly

Arsenal have moved on from their chase of Vinicius Jr after he signed a contract extension with Real Madrid and the Gunners have now reignited their interest in Atletico Madrid’s Julian Alvarez while PSG’s Bradley Barcola is also on their list.

But Bruno Guimaraes has finally officially completed his £75m move from Newcastle United with the deal for the 28-year-old midfielder representing a key piece of business of Mikel Arteta ahead of Arsenal’s title defence.

Rodri looks set to leave Manchester City amid interest from Barcelona and Real Madrid. The World Cup winning captain is into the final year of his contract and favours a move to Barca – though an initial offer of £38m has been rejected.

Liverpool, meanwhile, also want to sign Barcola from Paris Saint-Germain and have lined up his teammate Ibrahim Mbaye in what could be a double swoop for Andoni Iraola’s side. The European champions may be willing to let them go, especially following Maghnes Akliouche signing from Monaco, while the Reds also look to have secured much-needed defender help with ex-Barcelona captain Ronald Araujo set for a loan deal, with an option to buy, at Anfield.

Elsewhere, Manchester United have added to their ranks by bringing in a teenage midfielder and they are exploring their options at left-back with Lewis Hall reportedly now set on a move to Old Trafford, but Newcastle are determined to stop the exodus and insist he is not for sale.

The Red Arrows have been forced to pull out of a number of summer events in the UK after poor weather left them stranded in Canada.

The Royal Air Force (RAF) aerobatics display team are a popular fixture at air shows and military events around the country during the summer but they will not be able to fulfil three forthcoming engagements as their return across the Atlantic has been delayed.

They will not be performing at the Eastbourne International Airshow (13-16 August), the Royal Edinburgh Military Tattoo (ongoing until 29 August) and Lyme Regis Lifeboat Week (15-22 August).

open image in gallery The Red Arrows are a fixture of summer air shows ( AFP/Getty )

The Red Arrows’ single-engine Hawk aircraft have a limited range and cannot carry out air-to-air refuelling, the RAF said.

As such, crossing the Atlantic has to be done in stages and requires having the correct RAF support aircraft, including search-and-rescue cover and those carrying essential technical equipment, in the right place, at the right time.

Weather in north-east Canada has been “particularly challenging”, the air force said, adding that the team will now have to begin its multi-leg journey back to the UK from next week.

Other RAF aircraft will participate at the events in the UK.

open image in gallery The RAF Red Arrows have had to pull out of a string of summer events ( PA )

The Typhoon Display Team and Battle of Britain Memorial Flight (BBMF) remain part of the line-up at Eastbourne.

The BBMF is also carrying out flypasts at Lyme Regis during Lifeboat Week, on 21 and 22 August.

A C-17 Globemaster and two Typhoon jets will now perform a flypast over the Royal Edinburgh Military Tattoo on Saturday 15 August.

open image in gallery The Red Arrows perform a flypast over Windsor Castle during a state visit for US President Donald Trump on September 17, 2025 ( Getty )

A statement on the RAF website said: “The Red Arrows plan to continue a multi-leg journey back to the United Kingdom from North America next week (w/c 10 August).

“Due to a prolonged period of poor weather in the north-eastern regions of Canada, the team’s return from a tour of the United States was postponed last week.

“It is now anticipated this Atlantic crossing will be able to begin again from late next week based on more favourable conditions.

“Regrettably, this revised timeline means the Red Arrows will not be in a position to complete performances at Airbourne: Eastbourne International Airshow, the Royal Edinburgh Military Tattoo and Lyme Regis Lifeboat Week.

open image in gallery The the Red Arrows fly over the Mall towards from Buckingham Palace following the armed forces procession on 5 May 2025 to celebrate the 80th anniversary of VE Day ( AFP/Getty )

“All of these events remain on as scheduled with exciting line-ups and featuring other participating RAF aircraft.

Wing commander Sasha Nash, officer commanding RAF Aerobatic Team, added: “We are very sorry the Red Arrows cannot participate at these events and we are grateful to organisers and communities for their understanding.

“Every effort is being made to ensure the Red Arrows can recommence the busy display season as soon as possible.

“However, safety is the only factor that will determine the timing of the team’s return from Canada.”

The UK economy is expected to have recorded another quarter of growth as businesses find ways to cope with the fallout of the Iran war, but some industries are coming under increasing pressure, economists think.

Figures from the Office for National Statistics published on Thursday are set to show a degree of resilience in the economy in the face of supply chain issues and price pressures linked to the conflict, as well as a period of political uncertainty.

Some economists think gross domestic product (GDP) will have increased 0.4% for the second quarter, between April and June.

This would mean the economy has continued growing after a 0.6% rise in GDP for the first three months of 2026.

Rob Wood, chief UK economist for Pantheon Macroeconomics, said this would show “the big picture is that the economy has remained resilient to the hit from the war in Iran”.

open image in gallery

It comes as the services sector – the most dominant in the UK economy – strengthened in May, largely coming from professional services and scientific research and development.

Furthermore, recent data has pointed to factories and manufacturing firms stockpiling in anticipation of supply shortages and price rises, which has helped keep growth elevated.

But a weaker picture may be emerging from June as the heatwaves bring mixed results for businesses and some industries come under increasing pressure, economists said.

Mr Wood is expecting monthly GDP to dip by 0.1% in June, “reversing the 0.1% gain in May, as a sharp fall in construction activity drags on growth, while services and industrial production stagnate”.

open image in gallery England reaching the World Cup semi-finals is expected to have helped boost spending in July (Bradley Collyer/PA) ( PA Wire )

Thomas Pugh, chief economist for RSM UK, said he was expecting the services industry to have been dragged down by a fall in hospitality activity, despite the Fifa World Cup kicking off in June.

Mr Pugh said its own business surveys suggest “consumers were likely switching away from restaurants towards pubs to watch the World Cup, rather than increasing the total amount of spending”.

But he added: “There could still be a boost to activity in July, given the scorching weather and England reaching the semi-finals.”

Mr Pugh has a slightly more positive outlook for June, forecasting monthly GDP to have risen by 0.1%.

“All told, we expect GDP to nudge up in June, helped by a big jump in erratic mining activity,” he said.

“That will be enough to deliver 0.4% growth for Q2 (the second quarter), as strong momentum from Q1 (the first quarter) and consumers smoothing through higher inflation helped to support solid growth.”

A quarterly increase in GDP will likely be good news for new Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who has said he wants to achieve “growth in every postcode” of the UK.

He opened a new headquarters for the centre of Government in Manchester in late July, named No 10 North, where he is expected to work once each week as part of his move to push power out of Westminster.

Filip Nowacki admitted celebrating a breakout Commonwealth Games in Glasgow has been the farthest thing from his mind as he gears up for the European Aquatics Championships in Paris this week.

It has been a whirlwind past couple of weeks for the teenager, who claimed silver in the men’s 100 metres breaststroke, nudging mentor and three-time Olympic champion Adam Ramsay-Peaty into bronze.

Nowacki then went one better in his preferred 200m breaststroke, beating 2020 Olympic gold medallist Zac Stubblety-Cook, but the 18-year-old has barely had a chance to reflect on his seismic achievements.

Instead, Nowacki is targeting European honours, getting his campaign under way on Monday in the 100m breaststroke alongside Ramsay-Peaty, and he accepts that is part and parcel of a swimmer’s lot.

“No time to celebrate,” Nowacki told the Press Association. “After the Commonwealth Games, it’s always quite hard to settle back down to reality and it’s very important you do that as fast as possible.

“Because living on a high and living on that emotion is very taxing and it takes a lot of energy out of the system so now it’s just about recovering and getting the mind straight before diving back into it.

“Ultimately, all the hard work in the season has been put in, I can’t change how I’m going to swim apart from making sure my body’s fresh and my mind’s ready to go.”

Nowacki, the world junior 100m and 200m breaststroke champion, became the most decorated athlete in Jersey’s Commonwealth Games history with his two medals, claiming the island’s first gold in 36 years.

“I’m very proud of myself,” he said. “To step up on a senior international stage is challenging and there was a lot of pressure from Jersey that I didn’t quite feel beforehand.

open image in gallery Leon Marchand has withdrawn from the men’s 200 metres breaststroke in Paris this week (Peter Byrne/PA) ( PA Archive )

“But after both my races, I stepped back into my hotel room and I could finally breathe again – it was a massive weight off my shoulders, which I didn’t realise I had in the first place.”

A mouthwatering clash with Leon Marchand awaited Nowacki in the 200m breaststroke on Wednesday and Thursday, but an adductor injury has led to the four-time Olympic champion pulling out of the event.

“I’d love to race against him,” Nowacki said. “I’m always up for a race and that’s what’s very special: I get to race against the best in the world.”

While Nowacki will once again go up against Ramsay-Peaty in the 100m breaststroke, he clearly reveres the world record holder and takes every opportunity to speak to him in an effort to learn from him.

“I’ve looked up to him since he won his first Olympic gold medal in 2016, I must have been eight or nine and watching the replays on TV was special,” Nowacki added.

open image in gallery Adam Ramsay-Peaty will also be in action in the French capital this week (Andrew Milligan/PA) ( PA Wire )

“It’s nice to be racing against him in the lane next to him. I’ve got pictures of us both swimming breaststroke, an underwater shot, and I think that’s really cool. Had you told me that two years ago, I would have shaken my head in disbelief.

“He’s definitely played a massive role in my character development, especially from last year. I’ve spoken to him multiple times and I always try to extract as much experience from him as I can.”

Spanish authorities have announced the dismantling of a major people-smuggling operation, believed to have trafficked more than 2,000 migrants into the country and generated profits of €24 million (£20.5 million).

The network, described by Spain's Civil Guard as "one of the most complex, active and dangerous transnational criminal networks detected to date in the Mediterranean", used speedboats to transport synthetic drugs from Spain to Algeria.

On their return journeys, the boats then smuggled migrants to Spain's southeastern coast and the island of Ibiza.

The announcement comes as migration and human trafficking remain pressing concerns across Spain and Europe, following a mass border crossing into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta in late July, which saw 72,000 people enter the city.

Tens of thousands have since returned to Morocco, with many of those left behind setting up camp on the beach, while authorities have reported that the migrant reception centres in the city are overwhelmed.

Police believe the group, known for employing "extreme violence to protect its vessels", carried out at least 64 smuggling operations.

Members of the Spanish Guardia Civil patrol and conduct searches near a floating barrier off the border with Morocco ( Reuters )

Although the number of irregular migrants reaching Spain by sea fell 31 per cent in January-July, this was largely due to a 60 per cent drop in arrivals to the Canary Islands, Interior Ministry data showed.

By contrast, irregular migration to mainland Spain and the Balearic Islands rose 22 per cent and 10 per cent, respectively, over the same period as smugglers shifted routes via Algeria.

During the investigation, conducted with Europol and police in France, Portugal and Poland, authorities seized 18 speedboats and arrested 77 people in Spain and one in Algeria.

The network charged up to €12,000 (£10,000) per migrant and transported as many as 50 people on a single crossing, according to the statement.

The sea crossings were extremely dangerous, the Civil Guard said, with migrants travelling in overcrowded boats at high speed and often in rough seas, without lights, and, in most cases, life jackets.

"Sometimes the occupants were even tied down to prevent them from falling overboard during the crossing," the police said, adding that the organisation perpetrated extraordinary levels of violence against its own members and the migrants, as well as against police forces.

A leading expert on Bristol’s waterways has cast doubt on a leading police theory in the two-and-a-half-year investigation into the disappearance of Jack O’Sullivan.

For the past year, former harbour master Mike Ferguson has thoroughly reviewed the police’s long-held suspicion that Jack, then 22, fell into the River Avon after walking home from a night out with friends on 2 March 2024.

Since Jack disappeared, much of the investigation has centred on that possibility, but according to Mr Ferguson, the evidence says that conclusion is not possible.

In a detailed and independent report, Mr Ferguson evaluated tidal information and water temperatures of the night he went missing, as well as the extensive police search of the river that took place after Jack disappeared.

open image in gallery Jack O’Sullivan, left, went missing in March 2024 ( Catherine O'Sullivan )

Mr Ferguson, who has previously lent his expertise to police on missing person investigations, concluded it would have been “remarkable” if Jack wasn’t found during the search.

If Jack had fallen in, his body would have been caught in one of the catchment points where other bodies have previously been found, he added.

Police suspected he may have fallen into the river, as one of the last sightings of him on CCTV was near the water in the area of Brunel Lock Road and Brunel Way.

“The search that the police did was absolutely incredible,” Mr Ferguson said. “It was accurate; they searched at the right times in the right places. The assistant chief constable at the time described it as the biggest water search ever undertaken; I would agree with that.

“They were using masses of resources, and they would have found him.”

open image in gallery Mike Ferguson says it would have been ‘remarkable’ if Jack wasn’t found during the search, if he had gone into the water ( Mike Ferguson/Supplied )

The Independent set out last November to raise the vital funds needed to spread awareness of children who have gone missing and create SafeCall, a free and confidential support service designed to keep young people safe.

Thanks to the support of our readers and the backing of former prime minister Sir Keir Starmer, former footballer Sir David Beckham, the mother of missing Madeleine, Kate McCann, and many others, the helpline was launched in January after an incredible £165,000 was raised.

Jack’s mother, Catherine, believes Mr Ferguson’s findings give fresh hope over her son’s case, but claims the report was “totally dismissed” by police when she brought it forward to them.

“This is evidence, and if nothing else, [police] should be focusing their minds on something else [that could have happened],” she told The Independent.

Police said the information had been fed into its enquiries.

open image in gallery Catherine O’Sullivan is determined to find out what happened to her son ( Missing People )

Ms O’Sullivan remains determined to find out what happened to her son, and feels this could be key. She “doesn’t doubt that for a minute” that she could have answers if other theories had been more thoroughly investigated.

“We're living in a horrific day-to-day life because we have no idea what has happened,” she added.

She has always been sceptical about the theory that Jack fell into the water, and believes he got into a car instead.

“I feel that Jack's got into a vehicle... We know that's what his intention was because we see him approach a vehicle,” Ms O’Sullivan said. “We see him trying to get a taxi. His last message said he was getting a taxi.”

Ms O’Sullivan said she feels let down by Avon and Somerset Police's response to the disappearance of her son, which is now being reviewed by the College of Policing.

“We were told lessons would be learned, and, as I said to them, I'm really not interested in Jack being a lesson,” she said.

Assistant Chief Constable Joanne Hall said: “We wholeheartedly recognise the devastating impact Jack’s disappearance continues to have on his loved ones.

“We know how difficult it is for his family that, despite extensive enquiries, we’ve not yet been able to find him, or provide the conclusive answers they so desperately need.

open image in gallery Jack went missing after walking home from a night out with friends ( Catherine O'Sullivan )

“From the outset we’ve always had a shared aim of finding Jack and this intention has been at the heart of every action we’ve taken and decision we’ve made.

“Alongside our ongoing investigation, we’ve also drawn on specialist expertise and independent agencies to review, test and assure our work, ensuring that any further opportunities are fully explored. At every stage we’ve been led by the evidence and have pursued the relevant lines of enquiry.”

A spokesperson from the Missing People charity said: “Our hearts are with Catherine and her family. No family should have to live with the uncertainty of not knowing what has happened to someone they love. The not knowing can be one of the most painful and enduring experiences imaginable.

“At Missing People, we will continue to stand alongside Catherine and her family for as long as they need us. Whether that's providing emotional support, helping keep Jack's story in the public eye, or simply being there to listen, we remain committed to helping them find the answers they deserve.

“If anyone has any information about Jack, no matter how small it may seem, or believes they may have seen him, we urge them to contact Missing People on 116 000 or visit the web to share a sighting.”

Please donate now to The Independent and Missing People’s SafeCall campaign, which has raised £165,000 to create a free, nationwide service helping vulnerable children find safety and support.

For advice, support and options if you or a child you love goes missing, contact safecall.org.uk

The O’Sullivan family has set up a website, offering a £100,000 reward for anyone who has information on his disappearance.

News.title: Tens of thousands flee British Columbia wildfire as state of emergency declared
News.content:
Your support helps us to tell the story Read more Support Now From reproductive rights to climate change to Big Tech, The Independent is on the ground when the story is developing. Whether it's investigating the financials of Elon Musk's pro-Trump PAC or producing our latest documentary, 'The A Word', which shines a light on the American women fighting for reproductive rights, we know how important it is to parse out the facts from the messaging. At such a critical moment in US history, we need reporters on the ground. Your donation allows us to keep sending journalists to speak to both sides of the story. The Independent is trusted by Americans across the entire political spectrum. And unlike many other quality news outlets, we choose not to lock Americans out of our reporting and analysis with paywalls. We believe quality journalism should be available to everyone, paid for by those who can afford it. Your support makes all the difference. Read more

British Columbia has declared a state of emergency after tens of thousands were ordered to flee a fast-moving wildfire that nearly doubled in size overnight.

The Bald Range wildfire rapidly grew to about 9,500 hectares (23,500 acres), prompting evacuation orders in Summerland, Peachland and other districts west of Okanagan Lake in the southern interior.

The region produces most of B.C.'s wine and is Canada's second-largest wine-producing area.

Premier David Eby said Saturday that one fire official had likened the blaze, which is burning out of control, to "a bomb going off".

"He described flames on [a] 100-foot tree, flames going 200 feet above that, and the fire creating its own weather system, which creates lightning, which then feeds on itself," he said.

"Homes have been lost, and properties have been destroyed. Some people became trapped as conditions changed very quickly, and needed to be rescued."

open image in gallery Smoke rises from the Bald Range wildfire over a residential street in Summerland, British Columbia ( Reuters )

He added that it remained a very dynamic and threatening situation.

Summerland has a population of about 12,000 people, according to the 2021 census, and Peachland is home to about 6,500 residents.

A state of emergency grants the provincial government immediate access to special powers including travel restrictions and supply protections to prevent price gouging, and specific tools to coordinate rescue work.

Officials said the Bald Range wildfire triggered the largest evacuation event so far this summer and more than 20,000 people across B.C. have been forced to evacuate their homes.

open image in gallery The Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) block Highway 97 Northbound to direct people away from the Bald Range wildfire ( Reuters )

"A lot of farms have been affected. We don't know how many structures have been lost. They're still busy fighting the fire," Summerland Mayor Doug Holmes said.

"We have to brace ourselves for the worst."

‘You could see it behind the hills’

Many residents left overnight, driving south to Penticton or north to Kelowna before highways began to close.

Terry Fries of Summerland was watching a football game on Friday night when a neighbor advised him to get a bag ready as the fire grew.

"At the time, it was still farther back, and you could see it behind the hills," he said.

open image in gallery The hillside burns as residents evacuate towards Kelowna after midnight ( Reuters )

When B.C. authorities issued the evacuation order around midnight, he and his family drove about 45 km (28 miles) north to the city of Kelowna.

Residents recorded videos of fires by the highway and of structures burning as they evacuated. By Saturday afternoon, ashes began to settle on cars and houses in nearby areas as the fire painted the skies with orange hues.

Summerland lost power on Saturday and issued a boil-water notice for residents. The municipality said untreated water had entered the system after it bypassed the water treatment plant due to the wildfire.

Several Canadian provinces, including Ontario and Quebec, have battled blazes this year as hot, dry weather fueled wildfires in dense forest areas. Firefighters from Mexico, Australia, France and New Zealand have helped combat the fires.

In B.C., where hot and dry conditions have increased the risk of more fires spreading, about 1,500 firefighting personnel were battling more than 100 fires. The province has issued 40 evacuation orders and 49 alerts.

Fires have burned through 4 million hectares (9.9 million acres) in Canada this year, according to the Canadian Interagency Forest Fire Centre.
