World.title: Chinese Rafting Park in Hot Water Over ‘Female Companion’ Service
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018855/Chinese Rafting Park in Hot Water Over ‘Female Companion’ Service
World.content:
A river rafting tourist attraction in southwestern China has come under fire for offering “temporary girlfriends” and “very attractive” female companions who hold hands with, hug, and kiss customers while they raft.

Reported widely last week, the female companion service was offered by Luobei River Drifting, a popular rafting attraction in Guizhou province, beginning this summer. The rafting route, known for its thrilling rapids, lasts between 1.5 and 4 hours and covers up to 12.5 kilometers. Tickets cost up to 238 yuan ($35) per person.

In recent years, rafting attractions around China, including in the central Henan province, the eastern Jiangsu province, and the southern Hainan province, have launched scripted “NPC” rafting experiences, hiring workers to act as wolves, monkeys, bears, and frogs, as well as characters from the classic novel “Journey to the West” while customers raft. Related videos on Chinese social media have garnered tens of thousands of likes.

An undercover reporter at High Wind News, a platform under state-run media outlet Chinese Business View, posing as a customer contacted the attraction’s customer service on the messaging app WeChat, which informed them that they could choose from three service packages: a 398-yuan “highly attractive” companion who accompanies the rider with no additional physical contact, a 1,288-yuan partner with “upgraded appearance with polite physical contact,” and a 1,988-yuan “temporary girlfriend” option.

Customer service sent the reporter several photos — purported to be real pictures of the female companions — along with profiles of more than 30 women, including their height, weight, and age. Some photos were labeled “pure green,” indicating the companion’s service does not include “sexual behavior or contact.”

“The 1,988-yuan package is just like dating — you can hold hands, hug, and kiss,” the staff member told the undercover reporter, hinting that there could be further meetups after the initial rafting encounter.

“We create a legitimate setting for you to meet and communicate. We’re essentially just the intermediary,” the customer service representative added, claiming to receive around 400 groups of customers a day. The staff member also said the rafting park had more than 1,000 workers and required companions to be reserved in advance.

An account on Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok, by the name of “Luobei River NPC Scripted Drifting” had reportedly posted promotional videos of young women accompanying tourists during rafting and water activities, with slogans such as, “What heals you isn’t the scenery, but the emotional value.” The account has since been deleted.

Employees at the tourist attraction later confirmed to domestic media that companion services were available and directed reporters to the same customer service WeChat account.

In an official announcement posted on WeChat last Thursday, however, the company behind the park denied any connection to the female companion service, saying a separate company had privately launched the service.

A day later, on July 31, the local tourism bureau announced that Luobei River Drifting had agreed to collaborate with a management company specializing in upgraded rafting experiences, where tourists become the protagonists in stories instead of passive sightseers. According to the company’s official WeChat account, it had signed the cooperation agreement on May 6.

On July 31, the rafting operator was ordered by the local government to suspend operations for “rectification.”

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Female rafting companions. From Xiaohongshu)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018854/Check in, Log on, Stay for Months: Life at China’s 9-Cent Internet Café
World.title: Check in, Log on, Stay for Months: Life at China’s 9-Cent Internet Café
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018854/Check in, Log on, Stay for Months: Life at China’s 9-Cent Internet Café
World.content:
Outside an unassuming three-story building in downtown Kangyi Town, in the eastern Shandong province, hangs a sign that reads: “Striving to be the cheapest internet café in China.”

With charges as low as 0.6 yuan ($0.09) an hour, it’s certainly not false advertising. Yet step inside and you will find not just gamers chasing rock-bottom prices, but also a mix of locals and out-of-towners with myriad tales of misfortune, many looking to rise from their own rock bottom.

Here, customers can bathe and do laundry for free, enjoy a lunch of meat and vegetables for just 10 yuan, and even sleep in reclining esports chairs. For those looking to get back on their feet, it’s the ultimate low-to-no-cost option.

Like many of its patrons, the café’s owner, Wang Zhongkai, is also just trying to survive. After struggling to keep the doors open for more than a decade, the 38-year-old decided to slash his prices last year to attract more foot traffic.

The move certainly accomplished that — although it’s also inadvertently created a shelter for people in hard times.

After seeing a video about the internet café on Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok, Wang’s first out-of-town customer traveled 800 kilometers from neighboring Jiangsu province to “seek refuge” — and ended up staying for eight months.

Changing fortunes

China had roughly 122,600 licensed internet cafés last year, up 12% from 2024, according to the Internet Access Service Association of China. However, data from the Ministry of Culture and Tourism shows that average annual revenue fell from 216,000 yuan to 197,000 yuan over that same period.

Hardware is the biggest investment. With ever-changing technology, a new computer costing 15,000 yuan can lose a third of its value within a year, with software requiring constant paid-for upgrades.

Wang’s is one of only two surviving internet cafés in Kangyi. The business today has more than 150 computers of various specs, including 35 priced at 0.6 yuan an hour. The other machines in the main hall range from 0.9 yuan to 3 yuan an hour, while private one-person rooms are available for 99 yuan a day.

From nearly empty every day, Wang has seen occupancy increase to about 90%. At nighttime, the second floor is illuminated by the shifting colors of the PC screens, with the faces of customers — almost entirely men — aglow with yellow, green, red, and blue hues. Some are fast asleep, wrapped in summer blankets, headphones dangling from their neck.

Over the years, Wang, a father of three, has tried many ways to increase his income. He tried opening a grocery store on the side, which saw him lose 500,000 yuan in about six months. To recover, in 2023, he moved to Beijing — leaving his wife in charge of the café — to become a daijia, a designated driver for hire, working 15 hours a day. One day, he was so exhausted that he fell asleep while riding his electric bike and crashed.

He knows all too well that sometimes people just need to get through a rough patch. While living in the capital, he would pay 15 yuan to spend the night at an internet café where he could charge his e-bike and get hot water.

Wang returned to Kangyi in 2025. Today he helps his customers find low-cost rooms in town for as little as 200 yuan a month, with no deposit. For those who can’t even afford that, he lets them sleep for free in the café’s luxurious esports chairs.

He also advertises day-labor gigs available nearby, such as sorting packages at a courier depot or casual shifts at a machinery plant. Most of his customers decline, however, either because they’re not fit enough to handle manual labor or can’t stomach the idea of being bossed around.

His wife and mother-in-law are responsible for preparing lunch every day at the café, with one meat dish, one vegetable dish, and mountains of rice and steamed buns. Most diners pay 10 yuan, but those without a penny eat for free.

The showers and an industrial-size washing machine are also free to use — Wang even provides soap and detergent.

Despite the increased foot traffic, Wang’s profit margins remain wafer-thin. He says his family has invested more than 700,000 yuan in new computers, yet their revenue streams comprise only the cut-rate internet fees, sales of food and drink, and the occasional livestream on Douyin, during which some viewers will send virtual gifts. Except for relatives, the business has only one employee — an elderly male cleaner.

Boosting opportunities

Qiang Yu, a 30-something from Huaibei in the eastern Anhui province, has spent every day and night in the “0.6-yuan zone” for nearly a year. Like many others here, he makes money as a “game booster,” which involves playing video games to level up someone else’s account. His specialty is the online role-playing game Legend of Mir 2.

High-level accounts in popular games are worth tens of thousands of yuan, and cheating can lead to a permanent ban by game developers. Account owners are usually unwilling to hand their username and password to strangers, but Wang has built a reputation among several clients, offering a personal guarantee for any losses. He regularly farms out orders to the boosters at his internet café — and doesn’t even take a cut.

In the past, Qiang did manual jobs — digging gravel by the railway tracks, getting paid by the meter, his hands raw and blistered at the end of a shift, as well as toiling at factories making garments, lights, and electronics. It left him with a “crushing depression,” he says.

Qiang now earns just over 100 yuan for 12 hours’ work and survives on just 25 yuan a day. If, in a year, he has 10,000 yuan in his pocket, he plans to go home and clear the weeds that have taken over his courtyard.

Cao Ti Lie, a gamer who asked to be identified only by his username, arrived in Kangyi from Foshan, in the southern Guangdong province, in June. He grew up in video arcades, and now regularly livestreams to 60,000 subscribers on Douyin as he competes in the classic King of Fighters ’97.

Gaming used to be fun, he says; now it’s a full-time job. “The heart of the boy I was is dead. When you have to face life, it gets erased.”

The 41-year-old previously ran a business in Foshan and was making 30,000 yuan a month, but bad investments and a gambling habit saw his debts pile up. His wife left with their children, and then his mother suffered a stroke and broke her hip, losing the ability to care for herself.

Soon after spotting a video about Wang’s internet café, he hopped on a train here. His only goal is to save enough money to cover the costs of his mother’s nursing home.

Future is now

Wang’s day starts at 8 a.m. He scrubs five toilets, restocks the fridge, wipes down the keyboards, picks up any trash from the night before, and then takes his spot at the front counter.

He sees plenty of local faces come and go, but many of the out-of-towners are now permanent fixtures. In February, the café hosted about 40 people on Chinese New Year’s Eve, an important day on the calendar for family reunion.

Mao Lifen, a gamer from the northern Shanxi province who arrived in May, says he tries not to think about the future. He used to have a plan — work at a factory for five years, save up, and open a fruit shop. This was derailed when he and his colleagues had a falling out with the factory management and quit.

He went to work in food delivery and partnered with a friend to open a restaurant, maxing out several credit cards to the tune of 100,000 yuan and losing it all. Mao then tried starting a business with another friend, who ran off with all their money. A string of bad investments appears to have killed his interest in making plans.

His only thought now is to get through this year. “I’ve got food and drink — what is there to be unhappy about?” he says. At Wang’s internet café, he takes boosting orders for the first-person tactical shooter game Delta Force. When he’s not playing, he likes to walk up to the rooftop to look at the trees in the distance.

Mao likes this life that requires next to no human contact: everyone stares at their screen, submerged in the game. With his headphones on, there is no “outside world.”

This year, a wannabe entrepreneur from out of town visited Wang with a view to copying his business model elsewhere. Wang laid it out for him: 150 computers plus renovations, licensing, and other expenses mean at least 2 million yuan upfront; profits will unlikely keep pace with the equipment’s depreciation; and a minimum of three or four employees are needed to run 24/7. The visitor listened patiently and immediately abandoned the plan.

Wang knows he’s too deep into the industry to pull out. When he was young, he dreamed of making a fortune and owning a luxury car, but now “I know my limits,” he says. With a 30-year mortgage and still owing 110,000 yuan for equipment, his only wish is to draw customers and stay afloat.

(For privacy reasons, Qiang Yu and Mao Lifen are pseudonyms.)

Reported by Jiang Wanru.

A version of this article originally appeared in White Night Workshop. It has been translated and edited for brevity and clarity, and is republished here with permission.

Translator: Kiong Xin Xi; editors: Wang Juyi and Hao Qibao.

(Header image: Customers sleep in the esports chairs, at Wang’s internet café in Kangyi Town, June 2026. Jiang Wanru/White Night Workshop)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018850/A Chinese Coal City Finds New Use for Old Mines: Cooling Homes
World.title: A Chinese Coal City Finds New Use for Old Mines: Cooling Homes
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018850/A Chinese Coal City Finds New Use for Old Mines: Cooling Homes
World.content:
A Chinese city has launched a new residential cooling program using water from abandoned coal mines, a low-carbon initiative that could replace traditional air conditioners.

The initiative in the eastern Jiangsu province’s city of Xuzhou routes water from the now-defunct Woniushan Coal Mine to apartments in a nearby neighborhood, domestic media reported this week. The water maintains a consistent temperature of 19 degrees Celsius year-round.

Disused mines often fill with water via rainwater accumulation and groundwater seepage — water that can then be used to heat or cool nearby homes.

Xuzhou, a former coal-producing center with a decades-long mining history, has previously used abandoned mine water for clean heating, including a system installed last winter at its former Hanqiao Coal Mine. With annual average temperatures climbing and China’s “dual carbon” initiative — where the country aims to peak its carbon emissions by 2030 and achieve carbon neutrality by 2060 — a national priority, the cooling initiative, which began June 1, has been a focus for the city.

“After heat exchange (with the homes), the water returns to the mine, without having consumed any energy or produced any carbon emissions,” Zhang Tao, leader of the cooling project and a worker at Xukuang Heating Company, told state media outlet CCTV. Compared with traditional air conditioning, he said, this technology lowers carbon emissions and aligns more closely with China’s energy conservation and emission reduction policy.

According to domestic media, such closed-loop geothermal systems reduce energy consumption by approximately 50% compared with traditional methods. It is also estimated to reduce carbon dioxide emissions for the 100 homes in the pilot program by about 50 tons annually.

The city offered residents in the pilot program two free months of cooling, after which they’ll be charged quarterly at 4 yuan ($0.60) per square meter.

Wang, a resident in the pilot area, said that in previous summers her monthly electricity bill often exceeded 400 yuan due to air conditioner usage. In contrast, the pilot program has allowed her to cool her home for four months this summer for only 410 yuan. She said her home now maintains a constant temperature 24 hours a day, and the system is quiet, unlike air conditioners.

Zhang, the heating company researcher, noted the great potential of the pilot program. “This year we only used a part of Woniushan Coal Mine’s capacity, and since the mine has significant potential, in the future we plan on using it to capacity, extending it to more neighborhoods.”

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: VCG)

World.title: How PSG Academy’s Arrival Reflects Kazakhstan’s Rise as Football Talent Hub
World.content:
ALMATY – Paris Saint-Germain’s decision to open its first football academy in Kazakhstan this September is more than another international expansion for the French club. It reflects Kazakhstan’s growing attractiveness as a destination for elite youth football development, following a series of milestones that have elevated the country’s profile.

Located in Astana, the new PSG Academy Kazakhstan will welcome up to 300 boys and girls aged six to 14 during its inaugural season. Training will follow the official Paris Saint-Germain methodology, modeled on the club’s renowned youth academy in France and emphasizing technical excellence, game intelligence, discipline and teamwork.

While the academy’s opening marks Kazakhstan as the 24th country in PSG’s global network, it also fits into a broader pattern that has accelerated over the past two years: the country is increasingly positioning itself not only as a participant in international football, but as a place where future talent can be developed.

A broader football ecosystem is taking shape

The arrival of PSG follows several developments that together suggest Kazakhstan’s football strategy is evolving beyond isolated infrastructure projects or individual success stories.

Earlier, Atlético Madrid announced the creation of its football academy at the Akbulak Olympic Center in the Almaty Region. The project aims to introduce the Spanish club’s training methodology while improving the qualifications of Kazakh coaches and developing young players capable of competing at the highest international level.

Institutionally, Kazakhstan also reached an important milestone when the Kazakhstan Football Federation’s national academy became only the ninth association in the world and the second UEFA member to receive official FIFA Talent Academy recognition. The designation confirms that the country’s youth development system meets international standards and places Kazakhstan among a small group of national federations participating in FIFA’s global talent development initiative.

From exporting talent to building pathways

The growing interest from international clubs coincides with increased visibility of Kazakh football talent abroad. Earlier this year, teenage player Dastan Satpayev completed a record transfer to Chelsea, becoming one of the country’s most promising young exports.

Kazakhstan’s domestic football also enjoyed a breakthrough season. FC Kairat became the first Kazakh club to qualify for the UEFA Champions League group stage after eliminating Scotland’s Celtic FC in a dramatic penalty shootout in Almaty.

The club was later ranked among the world’s top 500 football clubs by the International Federation of Football History and Statistics (IFFHS), becoming the only Kazakh representative on the list.

Another milestone came when goalkeeper Anarbekov became the first Kazakh footballer to be named UEFA Champions League Player of the Match following his performance against Olympiacos. UEFA awarded him a 9.2 rating, while two of his saves were selected among the competition’s best moments of the round.

Taken individually, these achievements represent important milestones. Together, they suggest Kazakhstan’s football system is becoming increasingly visible within international scouting and development networks.

Why Kazakhstan?

For PSG, Kazakhstan offers more than a new commercial market. Football participation has grown steadily in recent years, accompanied by increasing investment in sports infrastructure and youth development. The Astana academy will initially operate from Air Arena, a modern indoor complex with a FIFA-standard pitch that allows year-round training despite Kazakhstan’s climate.

PSG also announced plans to expand beyond Astana, signaling that the project is intended as a long-term investment rather than a standalone academy.

“We are proud to bring the PSG Academy to Kazakhstan and provide young players with access to the Club’s world-class training methodology and football philosophy, “ said Almaz Alsenov, founder of PSG Academy Kazakhstan.

“Through this partnership, we aim to contribute to the long-term development of youth football in Kazakhstan by creating an environment where children can grow both as athletes and as individuals,” he added.

PSG officials similarly described Kazakhstan as part of the club’s strategy to broaden access to its football methodology worldwide while strengthening its international academy network.

Beyond international recognition

The arrival of another European football giant does not, by itself, transform Kazakhstan into a football powerhouse. Elite player development depends on far more than academy brands. Coaching quality, domestic competition, scouting systems and clear pathways from youth football to professional clubs remain equally important.

Yet the sequence of recent developments, from FIFA recognition and international partnerships to the emergence of players attracting attention from Europe’s top clubs, suggests Kazakhstan is gradually building many of those foundations.

If these initiatives continue to reinforce one another, the opening of PSG Academy Kazakhstan may come to represent more than the expansion of one of Europe’s biggest clubs. It could mark another step in Kazakhstan’s evolution from a country that occasionally produces exceptional footballers into one that is increasingly recognized as part of football’s global talent development ecosystem.

World.title: Back Where They Belong: Mangystau Helps Wild Birds Take Flight Again
World.content:
ASTANA — Kazakhstan’s first temporary rehabilitation center for injured birds of prey and endangered wild birds has opened in the Mangystau Region, providing veterinary treatment and rehabilitation before the animals are released back into their natural habitat.

The facility focuses on rescuing birds that have been injured or weakened, including eagles, falcons, hawks and other species protected under Kazakhstan’s Red Book. Specialists at the center conduct medical examinations, provide treatment and oversee rehabilitation until the birds are fit to return to the wild.

The project is now being implemented by the Umit Mangystau public foundation and commissioned by the region’s Department of Natural Resources and Environmental Management.

At the moment, the center is preparing four birds for release into the wild. They are a rare glossy ibis and three common kestrels. Before returning to the natural habitat, the birds were ringed by ornithologists, allowing researchers to track their movement and gather information about the condition of the local bird population.

For some of the center’s patients, it may take days and weeks of intensive care. Injured or severely weakened birds may arrive unable to feed on their own. In its social media post, the center explains that specialists initially feed such birds by hand, tailoring diets and feeding schedules. The center said the process of restoring independent feeding can take anywhere from several days to several weeks.

The Mangystau Region lies along one of the country’s most important migratory bird routes. Every year, thousands of birds pass through the region, including rare and endangered species. Many suffer injuries after colliding with power lines, vehicles and other infrastructure, while others fall victim to illegal hunting and trapping.

The initiative builds on years of volunteer work by wildlife advocates and veterinarians in Aktau, the region’s administrative center, who treated injured birds without dedicated funding. Among those involved in the effort were local blogger and volunteer Azamat Sarsenbayev and volunteer Natalya Inasaridze. Their work later drew the attention of regional authorities, leading to discussions to establish a specialized rehabilitation center.

The public is encouraged to report injured or exhausted wild birds to the center so they can receive timely veterinary care and, whenever possible, be returned to their natural environment.

World.title: Kazakhstan Expands Efforts to Revive Iconic Aport Apple
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan has launched a new phase of its effort to revive the iconic aport apple, a variety once renowned worldwide but now considered at risk of disappearing. Scientists are expanding orchards and establishing specialized nurseries to restore commercial production of the historic cultivar and supply growers with high-quality planting material.

The Kazakh Ministry of Agriculture leads the initiative in partnership with the country’s research institutions.

Unlike most commercial apple varieties, aport requires highly specific growing conditions. The trees thrive only at elevations between 850 and 1,250 meters above sea level, limiting cultivation to select foothill areas of Almaty and the surrounding Almaty Region. The variety is also slow to mature, typically producing fruit after eight to nine years, compared with four to six years for conventional apple orchards. Despite these challenges, aport remains highly valued in Kazakhstan for its distinctive flavor, large fruit, and historical significance.

The national Aport Revival Program, which runs from 2024 to 2028, aims to produce enough planting material to restart large-scale commercial cultivation. During the first stage in 2024, researchers collected seeds from the wild sievers apple, widely recognized as the ancestor of many modern cultivated apples, and began developing national cultivation standards for Kazakhstan’s aport variety.

According to Bakytzhan Duisembekov, chairman of the board of the Zhiembayev Kazakh Research Institute of Horticulture, restoring the variety has become one of the institute’s top scientific priorities.

“In 2015, we planted the first five-hectare ecological orchard of aport apple trees. Today, a program is underway to expand the area to 100 hectares,” Duisembekov said.

The next phase focuses on expanding nursery production to supply saplings to fruit growers nationwide.

“Creating nurseries will allow us to propagate the saplings and distribute them to our orchardists. This is how we can restore the former glory of the aport apple, which was once recognized worldwide,” he said.

Duisembekov noted that Kazakhstan has established a 10-hectare nursery where two-year-old saplings are being cultivated. Next year, they will be ready for planting in commercial orchards.

The broader initiative has received more than $5 million in funding, including around 500 million tenge (US$1 million) dedicated specifically to restoring the aport variety.

Researchers say expanding nursery production could eventually support the establishment of thousands of hectares of new orchards and help restore the country’s aport apple as one of the world’s most recognizable heritage apple varieties.

Last year, Scottish traveler and musician Ross Jennings visited Kazakhstan, inspired in part by the country’s reputation as the birthplace of the apple.

The article was originally published in Kazinform.

World.title: Five Doctors, One Race and Life Beyond the Hospital
World.content:
ASTANA — When former patients line up for the Jüregımnıñ Jeñımpazy (a champion of my heart) charity run in Astana on Aug. 9, some of the doctors who treated them will be at the starting line too. For five surgeons working across cardiac, transplant, neonatal and pediatric care, the race offers a rare chance to see what happens after some of medicine’s most complex operations – when patients return to everyday life.

Organized by the Heart Center Foundation (HCF), the annual event marks Kazakhstan’s first heart transplant, performed in August 2012, and raises awareness about organ donation and transplantation. This year, organizers expect more than 7,000 participants and visitors, with one, three, and 10-kilometer races.

The event comes as demand for transplantation remains high. According to HCF, 4,604 people, including 120 children, were on Kazakhstan’s transplant waiting list as of March 19. Transplants involving organs donated after death nearly tripled, from 23 in 2024 to 68 in 2025, yet 342 patients were unable to receive a transplant in time last year.

Behind the event are doctors whose work begins long before anyone reaches a starting line. They operate on premature newborns weighing only a few kilograms, perform and support complex transplant procedures, guide families through difficult decisions and, in some cases, know the experience of being a patient themselves.

Ahead of the race, five Astana surgeons spoke to The Astana Times about the experiences that have shaped them as doctors, and what it means to meet patients again when they are no longer in a hospital bed.

Seeing medicine from both sides

Cardiac surgeon Zhanna Rakish knows the doctor-patient relationship from both sides.

Having undergone kidney transplantation herself, she said becoming a patient changed the way she understood fear, uncertainty, and the trust people place in a medical team. Before her illness, she primarily saw disease as a problem that needed to be treated. Her own experience showed her what it means when life becomes organized around hospital visits, procedures and the hope of receiving a donor organ.

“For the team, an operation is a complex, well-practiced protocol; for me, it is always a kind of sacred act. I myself clearly remember that cold in the operating room, that feeling of fear of the unknown, and the boundless trust that you place in your colleagues. Therefore, every movement that I make here, everything I say to patients, comes with a clear understanding that in front of you is a person with hope that requires careful treatment. And something that was once given to me, I try to pass on to those people who come to me for help,” she told The Astana Times.

That memory, she said, now influences both her work in the operating room and the way she speaks to patients.

Last year, after Rakish completed the charity race, a parent approached her and said she had once treated their child. Following surgery, the family had been afraid to allow the child much physical activity and had treated the child, in Rakish’s words, “like a fragile vase.”

Seeing a doctor who had herself undergone transplantation complete the race helped change that perception. The parent told Rakish that her example had made the family less afraid of allowing their child to lead an active life.

“Those were very precious words, and from time to time I hear them again. They serve as a kind of support, a hope that none of this was in vain,” she said.

When the patient cannot speak

For neonatal and pediatric surgeon Zhenis Sakuov, some patients are only days old. Premature babies he operates on can weigh less than 2.5 kilograms, making precision essential throughout surgery and recovery.

“Operating on newborns, of course, requires particular precision and endurance. These patients are the most vulnerable, because operating on newborn babies is difficult, and operating on premature babies is even more difficult. The operation itself is complex, the management of the postoperative period is complex, and they need specialized care after surgery. Only by having a good team can you achieve success in neonatal surgery,” he told The Astana Times.

A newborn cannot describe pain or symptoms, leaving doctors to rely on examinations, laboratory tests and imaging. At the same time, parents may be trying to understand a serious diagnosis shortly after the birth of their child.

“The most difficult thing in our work, of course, is the conversation with the parents,” said Sakuov.

He highlighted that he encourages families to have another close relative present during important conversations and to prepare questions in advance, so they can better process the information they receive.

Outside the hospital, running has become another space in which Sakuov encounters people differently. He is part of a UMC running community and regularly participates in road and trail races.

During one 42-kilometer marathon, he found himself running for about half an hour beside a stranger who began speaking openly about difficult periods in his life.

“This is probably one of the forms of psychotherapy, because when you run for a very long time, all the unnecessary doubts and thoughts move into the background, and only you and the road remain. There is a kind of clarity in your head,” he said.

Meeting children years later

Pediatric cardiac surgeon Tlektes Nashkenov also works with patients whose small size can make every movement critical.

“When I was just starting out, the most unexpected thing for me was how small our patients can be and how enormous the responsibility for their lives can be. Sometimes it is a newborn weighing only a few kilograms, and you need to perform an operation where literally every millimeter counts,” he told The Astana Times.

Nashkenov noted that with experience he came to understand pediatric cardiac surgery not only as a technical discipline but as a combination of teamwork, continuous learning and communication with families.

“Parents entrust us with what is most precious to them – the life of their child. For them, it is important not only how the operation will go, but also to understand what is happening, what risks there are, and what the prospects are. We do not only treat the child; we accompany the whole family,” said Nashkenov.

He also said Kazakhstan can now perform procedures that previously required families to seek treatment abroad. Improvements in intensive care, diagnostics, anesthesiology and technologies such as extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) have expanded the options available for children with complex heart conditions.

Yet for Nashkenov, one of the clearest measures of success comes years after an operation.

“During treatment, we see a child at the most difficult moments of their life. And then, several years later, to see that child healthy, smiling, and running a marathon together with their parents – it is a very powerful emotion. It is the best confirmation that our work truly changes lives,” he said.

That long-term view of recovery is also what draws Nashkenov to the Aug. 9 race, which he plans to join himself. For him, meeting former patients at the starting line offers a chance to see them not as patients, but as children who have returned to active everyday life.

Different sides of the same surgeon

Cardiac surgeon Aigerim Kuzhakhmetova describes herself in the operating room as calm and focused. When a situation becomes critical, she tries to slow down mentally, assess the risks and think several steps ahead. Outside surgery, she says, her personality is noticeably different.

“In everyday life, on the contrary, I am more open and emotional. I love humor, active communication and movement. But these are not two different personalities,” she told The Astana Times.

For the past two years, that more playful side has appeared at the charity race, where Kuzhakhmetova has run dressed as Wonder Woman.

“Why did I choose her? Because Wonder Woman is the princess of the Amazons. And she was raised in a society of strong and independent women. For me, this is a parallel to what I do in the field of cardiac surgery. It might seem that this is a stereotypically male profession. But in fact, we have quite a lot of women who also work in surgical fields. And they can work on an equal level with men, be professionals, and show good results,” she said.

“When I was choosing an image for the run, I wanted to show that every person is a superhero. Every person who participates in this run is, in fact, a hero,” she added.

Her understanding of recovery is also shaped by patients she has seen regain abilities that illness had gradually taken away. Kuzhakhmetova recalled a woman under 40 who had severe respiratory failure before receiving a lung transplant. For several years, she depended on continuous oxygen and rarely left home. After transplantation and a long rehabilitation, Kuzhakhmetova later saw her walking through the hospital with her elderly parents.

What remained with the doctor was not only the patient’s recovery but her father’s reaction as he watched his daughter become independent again.

“We meet patients at one of the most difficult periods in their lives. And then at the starting line, we see them in a different role — as an active people, surrounded by their family and friends, with new plans and confidence in their own strength. I think that for every doctor this is a very important and inspiring moment, and it is also an indicator, a result of our work,” she said.

The challenge beyond the hospital

For cardiac surgeon Timur Lesbekov, transplantation also depends on what happens long before a patient reaches an operating room.

Having worked in the field since an earlier stage of its development in Kazakhstan, he remembers when donor coordination, organ retrieval and cooperation between medical teams in different regions required considerably more organizational effort.

Over time, those processes have become more established. Medical teams are more familiar with how quickly different services must work together once a potential donor process begins. At the same time, advances in organ preservation have reduced some of the logistical pressure created by Kazakhstan’s vast distances.

Despite these advances, he sees the main remaining obstacle as social rather than technical.

“The biggest difficulty is ourselves. I do not mean medical workers. I mean us as a society. The process is organized. We can work very quickly and effectively wherever in Kazakhstan a donor process is initiated. The main thing is for it to be initiated,” he said.

He does not see Jüregımnıñ Jeñımpazy as something that can directly solve the shortage of donor organs. Its role, he said, is to make transplantation and donation subjects that people are more prepared to understand and discuss with their families.

“It affects not only people’s awareness, it also affects whether a family begins to talk about donation. The decision we make can affect several lives in the future. And this is also a decision that everyone can make today,” he said.

For Lesbekov, the race also has a family history. His wife and children have supported the initiative since its earliest edition, when it began as a bicycle ride, and his daughter has volunteered with the foundation.

Their involvement has turned the event into a family tradition connected to a part of Lesbekov’s profession that can call him away from home without warning when a transplant process begins.

World.title: Is Kazakhstan’s Middle Class Expanding? New Survey Reveals More Than Just Income Trends
World.content:
ASTANA — More than 93% of Kazakh citizens describe their household’s financial position as middle income or above, according to a survey by the Bureau of National Statistics (BNS) released on Aug. 5.

The survey found that 70.1% of respondents described themselves as having an average level of material well-being, while 22.9% said they were somewhat above average. A further 4.9% considered themselves relatively well-off, and 0.3% described themselves as affluent. By contrast, only 1.8% assessed their financial situation as below average or poor.

These results come at a time when expanding the middle class has become a central element of Kazakhstan’s economic agenda, moving beyond a narrow focus on household income alone. In his 2024 State of the Nation Address, President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev stated that “economic growth should be accompanied by reduced social inequality and a strengthened middle class. Only in this way can we reinforce the country’s potential.”

This reflects a broader shift in economic policy thinking, where growth is increasingly assessed not only through GDP, investment, or industrial output, but also through whether it translates into higher living standards, better-quality jobs, and greater financial security for households.

Comparing 2023 and 2024: a shift in self-perception

BNS data from previous waves of the same survey suggest a modest shift in how Kazakh citizens position themselves within the income structure. In the earlier survey (2023), 74.2% of respondents identified as middle income, compared with 70.1% in the most recent 2024 results. At the same time, the share of those placing themselves above the middle has increased to nearly 23%.

Taken at face value, this could indicate a gradual rebalancing of self-perception, with fewer respondents identifying strictly as “middle” and more moving into the “above average” category. However, this should be interpreted cautiously. The change may reflect not only material improvements, but also shifts in expectations, inflation perceptions, or changing reference points for what households consider “average”. In other words, the data may suggest that Kazakh citizens are not only evaluating their income, but also redefining what “middle class” means in a changing economy.

Regional and demographic differences

The survey also highlights differences across regions and demographic groups. Among urban residents, 70.9% described their financial position as average, compared with 68.2% in rural areas. However, rural respondents were slightly more likely to identify themselves as relatively well-off (5.8%, compared with 4.6% in cities), while also being more likely to describe their situation as below average (3.2% versus 1.1%).

Men generally assessed their financial standing more positively than women. One quarter of male respondents said their income was somewhat above average, compared with 21.6% of women, while 5.7% of men and 4.5% of women considered themselves relatively well-off. This gap may reflect a mix of factors, including differences in income perception, social expectations, and variation in how respondents choose to self-report their financial status. Again, this is an interpretive observation rather than a statistical conclusion.

Beyond income perception, the survey indicates broadly positive attitudes toward household finances. 38.2% of respondents said they were satisfied with their financial situation, while 59.6% reported being partially satisfied. Only 0.5% said they were dissatisfied. Similar results were recorded for assessments of overall household economic conditions, with 39.6% fully satisfied and 57.9% partially satisfied.

Perception vs. objective indicators

The distinction between perceived and actual economic status is important because perceptions of prosperity do not always align with traditional macroeconomic indicators. A range of international research in behavioral economics and sociology, including work by the OECD, the World Bank, and studies published in journals such as the Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization, has shown that households often assess their financial well-being relative to expectations and to the living standards of those around them, rather than by income alone.

As living standards rise, expectations tend to rise as well, which can reshape how people define what it means to be “middle class.” This means that a stable or even improving economy can still produce shifts in self-assessment that do not directly mirror income growth statistics.

What the trend may suggest

Taken together, the comparison between 2023 and 2024 suggests a gradual shift in how Kazakh citizens locate themselves within the income distribution, with fewer identifying as strictly middle income and more placing themselves above that threshold.

Whether this reflects real income growth, inflation-adjusted improvements, or changing social benchmarks remains open to interpretation. However, the direction of self-perception combined with consistently high levels of reported financial satisfaction may indicate that Kazakh citizens are, at minimum, not experiencing a deterioration in perceived living standards, and may be gradually adjusting upward in how they define their economic position.

As policymakers continue to emphasize inclusive growth alongside headline economic performance, these perceptions may become an increasingly important lens through which they can understand how economic change is experienced on the ground.

World.title: EAEU Trade Nears $100 Billion as Bloc Shifts Focus to Digital Integration
World.content:
ASTANA — Trade among Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU) member states is on track to surpass $100 billion for the first time in 2026, as the five-country bloc shifts its focus from traditional market integration toward digital trade, artificial intelligence and the removal of non-tariff barriers. Speaking at the Eurasian Intergovernmental Council meeting in Cholpon-Ata on Aug. 7, Kazakh Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov said mutual trade within the EAEU reached $95 billion in 2025 and is expected to grow by 7.3% to $102 billion this year.

The milestone also reflects the bloc’s continued importance for Kazakhstan’s external trade. As previously reported by The Astana Times, trade with fellow EAEU member states reached $9.87 billion in the first four months of 2026, up 13.3% year-on-year. Russia remained Kazakhstan’s largest trading partner within the union, accounting for 87.6% of Kazakhstan’s trade with EAEU members, followed by the Kyrgyz Republic, Belarus and Armenia.

The discussions reflected what officials increasingly describe as the next stage of EAEU integration. While the bloc was initially built around the free movement of goods, services, capital and labor, policymakers are now focusing on digital integration, harmonized regulations and more efficient cross-border trade.

At the meeting, the prime ministers discussed measures to further develop the EAEU’s internal market, deepen sectoral cooperation and strengthen financial and economic coordination. The agenda also included the digitalization of freight rail transport and international transport corridors, e-commerce, climate cooperation and the integration of artificial intelligence into the union’s information systems.

The meeting concluded with the signing of six documents, including an Agreement on Electronic Commerce, aimed at creating a more unified regulatory framework for online trade, expanding opportunities for businesses and improving market access across member states. Participants also approved an agreement on the mutual recognition of academic titles and adopted several decisions aimed at advancing regional cooperation.

Rather than focusing primarily on tariff liberalization, the EAEU is increasingly prioritizing the removal of non-tariff barriers, digital customs and logistics, and common digital rules designed to make businesses more competitive across the union. For Kazakhstan, that next phase of integration also means addressing long-standing barriers affecting exporters.

Bektenov said Kazakhstan’s exports of animal and plant products, as well as processed food, reached nearly $7 billion in 2025 and totaled $3.6 billion in the first five months of this year. At the same time, he pointed to concerns raised by businesses over restrictions affecting poultry and dairy exports to EAEU markets.

Kazakhstan called for systematic monitoring of market access conditions for food products to ensure member states comply with their obligations under EAEU rules, arguing that a more consistent approach to resolving trade barriers would provide a significant boost to intra-union commerce. The proposal reflects a broader effort to address non-tariff restrictions, which have increasingly replaced customs duties as one of the main obstacles to deeper economic integration within the bloc.

Digital transformation emerged as another central theme of the meeting. The discussions build on commitments made at the Supreme Eurasian Economic Council summit in Astana in May, where member states adopted a Joint Statement on the Responsible Development of Artificial Intelligence. Speaking at that summit, President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev called for integrating national digital systems to accelerate customs procedures, identify bottlenecks and forecast cargo flows in real time.

“New technologies should not become the cause or source of digital gaps. They are designed to become an instrument of economic interconnectedness and powerful synergy of cooperation between our countries,” Tokayev said.

In Cholpon-Ata, Bektenov also highlighted Kazakhstan’s own digital ambitions, noting that 2026 has been declared the Year of Digitalization and Artificial Intelligence. Among the country’s flagship projects is the planned Data Center Valley in Ekibastuz, where the first 125 megawatts of computing capacity is scheduled to come online in June next year.

“The project will create digital infrastructure of international standards and strengthen Kazakhstan’s position as one of Eurasia’s digital hubs,” Bektenov said, inviting businesses and technology companies across the EAEU to participate in the initiative.

The meeting also reflected Kazakhstan’s close economic ties with fellow member Kyrgyzstan. During a collective meeting with Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov, Bektenov conveyed greetings from President Tokayev and noted that bilateral trade between Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan has doubled over the past five years to $2.2 billion, with both governments continuing efforts to expand commercial ties.

The next meeting of the Eurasian Intergovernmental Council is scheduled for Oct. 1-2 in Minsk, Belarus, where member states are expected to continue advancing the bloc’s digital integration agenda.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s Services Exports Near $13 Billion as Digital Sector Gains Momentum
World.content:
ASTANA — Kazakhstan’s services exports approached $13 billion in 2025, with transport remaining the backbone of the sector. But while logistics continues to generate nearly half of the country’s services export revenue, the fastest growth is increasingly coming from digital industries, pointing to a gradual shift toward higher-value exports.

According to Energyprom.kz, Kazakhstan exported $12.8 billion worth of services in 2025. Transport services remained the country’s largest export category, generating $5.7 billion, or 44.8% of total services exports, up 5.2% from a year earlier. Freight transportation accounted for $4.5 billion of that total.

Travel-related services ranked second, increasing 12.4% to $2.9 billion, driven largely by spending by foreign visitors traveling to Kazakhstan for tourism, education, medical treatment and personal visits.

Sustaining that growth, however, will also require continued investment in logistics infrastructure. In a report, the Eurasian Development Bank (EDB) identified modern warehousing as one of Central Asia’s biggest untapped opportunities, estimating demand for nearly 2 million square meters of new warehouse space and investment needs of up to $1.5 billion.

EDB Chief Economist Evgeny Vinokurov said in an interview with The Astana Times that Kazakhstan is particularly well positioned to capitalize on the trend due to its location at the intersection of major Eurasian trade routes.

“Kazakhstan is particularly well-positioned. Where North-South and East-West routes intersect, synergies emerge. We see at least three major logistics nodes: Almaty, Astana and Shymkent with strong potential for warehouse development,” he said.

But transport is no longer the whole story

Among the major service categories, telecommunications, computer and information services recorded the fastest growth, rising 35.6% to $1.4 billion. Together with transport and travel, the three categories generated nearly 78% of Kazakhstan’s total services export revenue.

The biggest breakthrough came from computer services. Their exports climbed 36% to $1.1 billion, surpassing the $1 billion mark for the first time. Even excluding digital asset mining, which accounted for $367.6 million, computer services exports reached $775.1 million, reflecting continued expansion of Kazakhstan’s technology sector.

The milestone also fulfills a strategic objective set several years ago. In his 2023 State of the Nation Address, President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev called for Kazakhstan’s IT services exports to reach $1 billion by 2026, identifying digital industries as one of the country’s future growth engines. The latest figures indicate that the target has effectively been achieved ahead of schedule.

Much of that growth has been supported by Astana Hub, whose resident companies exported IT services worth $681 million in 2025 to 111 countries, underscoring the expanding global footprint of Kazakhstan’s technology sector. According to previously reported data, the innovation hub is now home to more than 1,700 companies and continues to serve as the country’s primary platform for technology exports. Maintaining that momentum, however, may prove more important than reaching the milestone itself.

Computer services exports also remain highly concentrated geographically. Astana accounted for more than 90% of the country’s total, exporting around $1 billion worth of computer services in 2025. The concentration reflects the capital’s growing technology ecosystem, centered around Astana Hub and the newly launched International AI Center Alem.ai. Together, Astana and Almaty generated more than 96% of Kazakhstan’s computer services exports.

The figures suggest Kazakhstan is gradually broadening its export base. While transport continues to capitalize on the country’s strategic location at the crossroads of Eurasian trade routes, digital services increasingly demonstrate its ability to compete through innovation, technology and human capital.

The shift also reflects broader changes in the global economy. According to the OECD, services generate more than two-thirds of global GDP and attract more than three-quarters of foreign direct investment in advanced economies. Increasingly, countries compete not only by exporting physical goods, but also by selling knowledge, software, financial services and other high-value expertise.

For Kazakhstan, that transformation carries significance beyond the technology sector. Expanding services exports is increasingly viewed as a key pillar of economic diversification, reducing dependence on commodities while creating higher-value jobs, boosting productivity and strengthening the country’s long-term competitiveness.

The momentum continued into 2026. During the first quarter, Kazakhstan’s services exports increased 14.1% year-on-year to $3.1 billion, while imports rose 8.8% to $3.3 billion. As export growth outpaced imports, the country’s services trade deficit narrowed by 34.5% to $219.1 million. Transport remained the largest contributor, with exports rising 20.7% to $1.6 billion, while travel-related services increased 10% to $559.5 million.

Services are central to economic transformation

While transport remains Kazakhstan’s largest services export today, the country’s fastest long-term growth is increasingly coming from digitally delivered services. That shift mirrors broader changes in the global economy. WTO Director-General Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala has described services as “the fastest growing component of world trade over the last two decades,” adding that the digital revolution has “super-charged this trend.”

“Services are now central to economic transformation in developing countries. That is why mainstreaming services into national development strategies is no longer optional. Services are a necessity for diversification, productivity and resilience,” she said.

According to the WTO’s latest forecasts, digitally delivered services are expected to grow by 5.6% in 2026, significantly outpacing transport services, whose growth is projected to slow to 1.8%.

For Kazakhstan, the trend signals that the country’s next stage of export growth may increasingly depend not only on moving goods across borders, but on exporting technology, innovation and specialized expertise. If transport reflects Kazakhstan’s geographic advantages, the rise of digital services points to something equally important: the country’s growing ability to export knowledge and compete in the global economy through human capital rather than natural resources alone.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s Copper Output Places It Among World’s Top 10 Producers
World.content:
ASTANA — Kazakhstan ranked among the world’s 10 largest copper producers in 2025 after mining 710,000 tons of the metal, reinforcing its position in a market where demand is expected to accelerate as countries expand clean energy and digital infrastructure.

According to data from the Energy Institute (EI) and the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS), Kazakhstan shared ninth place with Indonesia, with both countries producing 710,000 tons of copper last year.

Chile remained the world’s largest producer with 5.3 million tons, followed by the Democratic Republic of the Congo with 3.2 million tons and Peru with 2.7 million tons. China ranked fourth with 1.8 million tons, while Russia produced 1.3 million tons. The United States (US), Zambia and Australia also ranked ahead of Kazakhstan.

Together, the world’s 10 largest producers mined 18.39 million tons of copper in 2025, accounting for the bulk of global output, which reached 23 million tons, according to the Energy Institute.

Kazakhstan’s ranking comes as demand for copper continues to rise. According to the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD), global demand for the metal is projected to increase by more than 40% by 2040, driven by the expansion of renewable energy, electricity grids, electric vehicles and digital infrastructure. Meeting that demand could require around 80 new copper mines worldwide, underscoring growing concerns over future supply.

Copper is widely used in power transmission networks, electric motors, batteries, solar panels, wind turbines and other technologies underpinning the global energy transition. As a result, it has become one of the minerals increasingly classified as critical for economic security and industrial development.

The latest ranking also aligns with Kazakhstan’s broader strategy of positioning itself as a reliable supplier of critical minerals. As previously reported by The Astana Times, the country has expanded partnerships with the European Union, the United Kingdom, the US and other international partners to attract investment, boost geological exploration and strengthen critical mineral supply chains.

With global competition for critical minerals intensifying, Kazakhstan’s place among the world’s top copper producers reinforces the country’s growing role in supplying one of the key resources needed for the energy transition and advanced manufacturing.

World.title: Is Wildberries moving to Kazakhstan?
World.content:
Wildberries is building warehouses in Kazakhstan

Based on reporting by Novaya Gazeta Europe

Wildberries is building warehouses in Astana and Almaty with a combined area of more than 260,000 square meters, Kazakhstan’s Minister of Trade and Integration, Arman Shakkaliyev, said.

Details.According to the minister, Wildberries is building a warehouse of more than 100,000 square meters near Almaty. Another facility, covering 160,000 square meters, is under construction in Astana. Both are scheduled to begin operations in the first quarter of 2027.

The company also already leases about 46,000 square meters of warehouse space in Kazakhstan.

Shakkaliyev said the ministry had received no formal request from Wildberries regarding the opening of new warehouses in Kazakhstan. He added that companies can negotiate directly with warehouse owners without government involvement.

Confirmation from Russia’s foreign ministry. Moscow and Astana began working to integrate their online marketplaces before Ukrainian attacks on Wildberries warehouses, Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Mikhail Galuzin said.

According to Galuzin, hundreds of thousands of Kazakh suppliers are already registered on Ozon and Wildberries.

Galuzin did not provide details of the deals, instead suggesting that questions about the companies’ specific plans be directed to their representatives.

Context. On July 29, Kommersant reported that Wildberries was looking for warehouse space in Kazakhstan following drone attacks on logistics centers in Russia. According to the newspaper’s sources, the company was prepared to take virtually all available warehouse space in Kazakhstan, where supply is generally limited. The move would allow the online retailer to shield part of its logistics capacity from drone strikes.

According to Kommersant, Wildberries is also continuing to search for new warehouse space in Russia. But owners of vacant facilities are currently reluctant to sign new leases with the company because of the risk of drone attacks.

World.title: Relatives of missing Russian soldiers demand that the state search for them. In response, they are accused of working for Ukrainian intelligence
World.content:
Missing Russian Soldiers

The Russian state sends soldiers to fight in its war against Ukraine, but once they go missing, it effectively disclaims responsibility for their fate. Families spend months trying to determine whether their loved ones have been killed, taken prisoner or are being treated in hospitals, only to encounter a closed and dysfunctional system for tracing the missing.

When relatives band together and demand answers, the authorities respond not with assistance but with pressure and accusations that they are cooperating with Ukrainian intelligence services.

Based on reporting by Novaya Gazeta Europe

A grassroots initiative called The Missing Regiment is gaining traction on Russian social media. Launched in the Yaroslavl region in the spring of 2026, it brings together relatives of Russian servicemen who have gone missing in the war against Ukraine. They are demanding that the state make a genuine effort to find the soldiers it sent to the front and tell their families what happened to them.

Although Russian law provides a mechanism for tracing missing servicemen, in practice it barely functions. Relatives say the agency responsible has no website, telephone number or publicly accessible address where families can submit inquiries. They believe it exists largely on paper.

A reporter for Veter spoke with activists from The Missing Regiment. Their stories illustrate how the Russian state leaves the families of missing soldiers without information — and what happens to those who publicly speak out about the system’s failure to act.

Missing in action

Groups dedicated to finding missing soldiers have existed on social media since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The information is typically posted by soldiers’ mothers, wives and sisters, who hope their messages will reach someone who knows what happened to their missing relatives.

Thousands of names and photographs have been posted in groups on VKontakte and Telegram. The images show former factory workers, security guards, prisoners, older men and men barely out of their teens.

Roman Artamonov, a 19-year-old from Saratov, began his compulsory military service on June 23, 2025. His unit was stationed in Borzya, a town near Russia’s borders with China and Mongolia. Two months later, he signed a military contract. After four months of training in Rostov, Roman was sent on a combat mission in the Donetsk region. Two days later, his family lost contact with him.

“Three months later, my son’s military unit declared him dead, citing Certificate No. 1421,” his mother, Elena Pisakina, said. “The document states that neither his body nor my son himself has been found. Searches among prisoners of war and in hospitals have yielded no results.”

Under Russian law, military commanders are required to declare a serviceman who has disappeared missing in action. The search must continue for six months. Only after that period can a court formally declare the person missing.

A serviceman can be declared dead immediately only if there is compelling evidence that the circumstances of his disappearance were life-threatening. The distinction also has financial consequences: during the six-month search period, the serviceman’s family continues to receive his military pay.

In practice, commanders therefore often seek to have missing soldiers declared dead as quickly as possible. Families do not always object. Once a serviceman is officially declared dead, relatives may be eligible for payments of about 10 million to 15 million rubles, depending on the region.

According to Mediazona, Russian courts received 90,000 such claims between 2023 and 2025, seeking to have servicemen legally declared missing or dead. Military unit commanders filed 26,000 of the claims, while agencies under the Defense Ministry filed another 20,000. In nearly 40,000 cases, information about the plaintiffs was withheld.

But having a soldier declared dead does not mean the search will continue, that the body will be returned or that a funeral will take place. Roman Artamonov’s family has still not been able to bury him.

Elena appealed to the military prosecutor’s office but received no explanation. She then took her story to social media. Her video was published by The Missing Regiment on its Telegram channel.

The movement emerged in April 2026 as an association of families of missing servicemen. Residents of other Russian regions soon joined the activists in Yaroslavl.

Members of the initiative help relatives draft appeals to Russia’s Investigative Committee, the presidential administration, the Red Cross and other organizations. Lawyers they know provide free consultations, and the activists also work with veterans’ groups.

On May 9, the movement organized small demonstrations in several cities, where relatives gathered holding photographs of missing soldiers.

But a grassroots initiative cannot search for people in a combat zone. It lacks both the authority and the resources to do so. Instead, activists collect names and photographs, building a virtual database of the missing. They say more than 9,000 people have already contacted them.

“An assault soldier is just a number”

After a serviceman disappears, commanders are required to determine whether he went missing during a mission or left his unit without authorization. In the first case, the military must conduct an internal investigation. In the second, the soldier can be placed on a wanted list, face criminal charges and have his payments suspended.

But commanders have used this provision as a loophole. According to Important Stories, soldiers who disappear during combat missions are routinely classified as having left their units without authorization — even when there is evidence that they were killed in battle.

If a serviceman is officially declared missing in action, his information is entered into a centralized database, including the location where he disappeared and witness testimony. Special search teams are then supposed to work alongside civic and volunteer organizations to locate the missing.

Bodies that are recovered are evacuated and identified visually, through fingerprints or DNA testing. Military enlistment offices are then supposed to inform relatives of the results.

In practice, the system works differently. According to Verstka, soldiers are warned before being sent to the front that they may not be evacuated — whether they are wounded or killed.

The recovery of bodies depends on conditions on the battlefield and on commanders’ decisions. The speed of the search also depends on the dead soldier’s rank. Officers are searched for and evacuated more quickly.

“How do they treat some assault soldier who gets killed somewhere? He’s just a number. We report the number to the division and forget about him,” a military source told Verstka.

Relatives often have no way of finding out who is searching for their loved ones, where the searches are taking place or how they are being conducted. Their only options are to contact military enlistment offices and wait for news from volunteers.

In the fall of 2025, the Defense Ministry established a Main Coordination Center. Formally, it is responsible for coordinating the work of government agencies, civic organizations and volunteers.

Families are advised to contact military enlistment offices, the Defenders of the Fatherland Foundation, the human rights ombudsman or the military prosecutor’s office. They can also submit an electronic request through the Defense Ministry’s website. But there is no way to contact the coordination center directly.

Activists believe the center exists only on paper. It publishes no reports and has no dedicated website, telephone number, email address or public office where families can seek help.

Members of the movement say the Defense Ministry has effectively shifted responsibility for the searches to regional military enlistment offices, which lack the necessary equipment, specialists and access to up-to-date DNA databases.

Still, ombudsmen have reported some results. In 2025, they helped locate more than 300 servicemen, and about 100 more were found in the first half of 2026. Most were either prisoners of war or soldiers being treated in hospitals.

Photo: Unknown Regiment / Telegram

Vladimir Putin has claimed that the creation of the center improved the situation. In December 2025, he said the number of servicemen being sought had fallen by 50 percent and had dropped threefold since the beginning of the year. But the source of those figures is unclear. Russian authorities conceal the true scale of the country’s military losses, including the number of soldiers who are missing.

The Ukrainian project I Want to Find accepts inquiries from relatives of Russian servicemen and checks the information against its own database of prisoners of war and the dead. According to Verstka, the project received more than 84,000 requests over the course of a year.

Going It alone

Anna, whose name has been changed, joined the movement after her brother went missing. He was serving under contract with the 119th Guards Airborne Regiment.

In June 2026, Anna found The Missing Regiment on social media and became an activist. She stresses that the movement does not oppose the war or criticize the authorities. Its sole aim, she says, is to determine what happened to missing servicemen.

“Women come to memorials and say that their son, husband or brother is missing,” Anna said. “They want to know what happened to him. Government agencies should be doing this work instead of sending relatives from one office to another. On paper, there is a system in place, but in reality it either does not work or works poorly.”

Within a few months, activists had emerged in many regions across Russia. The movement has been particularly active in the Lipetsk, Yaroslavl and Rostov regions.

A community event by the Unknown Regiment. Photo: Unknown Regiment / Telegram

One of the movement’s organizers is believed to be Mikhail, a businessman from Yaroslavl whose name has also been changed. He describes himself simply as an active participant.

Mikhail’s friend Sergei went missing in the combat zone. Sergei’s elderly mother was left to navigate the bureaucracy on her own and was unable to do so.

Mikhail and Sergei’s mother repeatedly contacted his military unit but received no answers. Unit officials said Mikhail was not a relative of the missing soldier and therefore had no standing to seek information. The local military enlistment official avoided both Mikhail and Sergei’s mother. When Mikhail tried to stop the official to speak with him, he was threatened with police action and a fine.

There were many similar stories. What began as meetings with relatives eventually grew into a broader initiative. Activists started publishing video appeals, portraits of missing servicemen and announcements of public gatherings.

They sought support from political parties and state-affiliated organizations, but United Russia showed no interest in the initiative.

The activists also tried to work with the Defenders of the Fatherland Foundation, which is headed by Anna Tsivileva, a relative of Vladimir Putin. But according to Mikhail, the foundation is seeking to monopolize the issue without providing an effective system for finding the missing.

The movement then approached Communist Party branches in the Krasnodar region and the Chelyabinsk region. The party had previously provided meeting space to wives of mobilized soldiers from The Way Home movement.

But the authorities have cracked down hard on attempts by soldiers’ relatives to organize. The movement of mobilized soldiers’ wives initially supported both the war and Putin. Later, its most active members were designated “foreign agents” and faced criminal prosecution, while others were intimidated into silence.

Cooperation with the Communist Party also came to nothing. Its branch in the Chelyabinsk region said it had not worked with the organization, while the Krasnodar branch did not respond to a request for comment.

The party tried to involve the movement in its campaign against internet restrictions. But the issue had nothing to do with the search for missing soldiers, and the cooperation ended.

A local branch of the New People party in the city of Shakhty initially expressed interest in the initiative. Soon afterward, however, its representatives stopped responding. Some activists believe this happened after consultations with law enforcement agencies. The party did not respond to a request for comment from Veter.

“Give people hope”

Despite the stance taken by political parties and state-affiliated foundations, interest in the initiative continues to grow. Mikhail says the movement is receiving an enormous number of requests for help.

“We want the search effort to be taken to a new level and for officials to stop withholding information,” he said. “Commanders and military enlistment officials need to stop sending relatives from one office to another. Right now, if we want to find out what happened to someone close to us, we are treated as enemies of the state.”

Mikhail says the uncertainty is tearing families apart. Sergei’s mother begins to cry every time someone asks whether there has been any news.

The activists believe the system cannot be changed without the state’s involvement. Political parties, they say, could appeal directly to the president and the government, paving the way for legislative changes.

But military enlistment offices have little interest in conducting searches, while commanders are focused on the war. Without a clear legal obligation to act, the activists say, the system will not work.

A prank that spun out of control

Even these nonpolitical demands are treated by the Kremlin as a threat. Pro-government outlets quickly portrayed the movement as a project run by Ukrainian intelligence services.

In June 2026, War on Fakes, Lapsha Media and Southern News Service claimed that the initiative was part of an information operation. According to their account, Ukrainian intelligence services were collecting relatives’ personal information in order to hack their accounts and extort money from them.

Southern News Service claimed that those behind the effort were seeking to instill a sense of abandonment and helplessness among relatives. The supposed goal, it said, was to spread the idea that the state was not searching for the missing and that only grassroots organizing and public demonstrations could help.

Ahead of May 9, schools in several Russian regions held lessons titled “The Missing Regiment: Memory Cannot Be Blocked.” The classes focused on missing servicemen and contained no political appeals.

Several days later, schools began removing information about the lessons. The Sota project then reported, citing an anonymous source, that the campaign had supposedly been a prank.

None of Russia’s well-known pranksters claimed responsibility. Activists insist that the lessons had been organized by teachers through prior arrangements. They say educators began facing punishment after the events and that the initiative was subsequently portrayed as a prank in an effort to discredit it retroactively.

According to Mikhail, the movement faces pressure not only from pro-government media but also from law enforcement agencies.

On June 6, activist Irina Chebotareva in Lipetsk stopped responding to calls and messages. She had spent a long time searching for her missing husband and was regarded as the movement’s local coordinator. Members of the initiative believe she may have been in police custody. Veter was unable to determine what happened to her.

In Shakhty, in the Rostov region, members of the movement joined a May 9 motorcade carrying portraits of their missing relatives. On June 12, they organized a small demonstration of their own.

Shortly before the event, police summoned the movement’s local coordinator, Valeria Klyuchnikova, and questioned her over possible involvement in terrorist activity. Officers told her that the motorcade had to be approved by the city administration and law enforcement authorities.

Klyuchnikova was later detained while picking up a package containing the movement’s flag and several T-shirts. Police confiscated the flag and one T-shirt before releasing her.

This article was produced with the support of Media Network

World.title: Armenian Catholicos Garegin II attends first hearing in criminal trial
World.content:
Catholicos of All Armenians appears in court

A court in Armenia‘s Armavir region has begun hearing the criminal case against the Catholicos of All Armenians and six bishops who serve on the Supreme Spiritual Council. Garegin II attended the hearing in person.

Clergy members and politicians gathered outside the courthouse. Lawmakers from the opposition Armenia Alliance and I Have Honour Alliance left parliament during the afternoon and travelled to Etchmiadzin to show their support for the Catholicos. Dozens of worshippers also gathered outside, periodically chanting “Your Holiness” and singing traditional Armenian church hymns (sharakans).

Prosecutors accuse the Catholicos and the senior clergy of obstructing the enforcement of a court ruling.

Garegin II removed Bishop Gevorg Saroyan, head of the Masyatsotn Diocese, from his post. Saroyan is one of the senior clerics who joined Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan’s campaign to “reform the Church”. The bishop challenged his dismissal in court. The court ordered his temporary reinstatement as head of the diocese until it reaches a final decision in the case. However, before the court could rule on the merits, the Supreme Spiritual Council, led by the Catholicos, also defrocked him. The council argued that the courts have no jurisdiction over the Church’s internal affairs.

Lawyer Ara Zohrabyan says the Catholicos faces criminal prosecution for carrying out his “ecclesiastical and canonical duties”.
