Angry football associations expressed outrage at the $US4.2 billion proposal, with the European federation threatening legal action and demanding Infantino and Kushner retain all documents relating to the proposal.

Even world leaders expressed their disapproval, including new UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, while Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said he has "no confidence" in the FIFA boss.

Clearly, passions run higher in football than politics, because Infantino ended up junking the plan as questions mounted about his future in football’s top job. The outrage at Trump’s dealings has been far more muted.

While Trump is facing enormous challenges in the upcoming mid-term elections, they are mostly related to the Iran war and the rising cost of fuel in the US.

Complaints about his family's business dealings at home and abroad, on a scale never before seen, have gained little traction outside the political sphere.

So far, about half a dozen firms are believed to have signed up to the plan to receive early access to presidential decrees via Truth Social. But their identities have remained under wraps.

Trump Media and Technology Group spokespeople have dismissed claims of irregularity, arguing the information is public and that other social media operations offer similar services.

But there are differences. Subscribers to the new Trump service will receive access to messages a fraction of a second before the rest of the world.

That may sound inconsequential. But in a world of high-frequency trading run by computers working off algorithms and increasingly powered by artificial intelligence, every nanosecond counts.

While other social media platforms offer similar services, they are mostly for back-end data rather than news-breaking pronouncements from a sitting president who owns 41 per cent of the company releasing the information.

The US president has regularly stated he has no control over his private companies, including the media group that his son Don Junior controls via a trust.

Donald Trump Jr (left) controls the Trump Media and Technology Group via a trust. (Reuters: Brendan McDermid)

Few experts, however, are convinced the links are adequately severed.

"I'll be blunt," Gian Luca Clementi, an economics professor at NYU Stern School of Business, told Fortune magazine.

"This is insider trading by definition."

Oiling the wheels of finance

It took barely a minute to complete.

On Monday, March 23, at 6:49am New York time, a huge volume of oil futures contracts was pushed through the market.

By 6:50am, about $US580 million worth of contracts covering Brent crude, the global benchmark, and West Texas Intermediate changed hands, sending prices into free fall, dropping from just under $US100 a barrel to $US89.

The trading volume was around nine times the normal level with precise bets on the direction of both oil and equity markets.

Within minutes, Donald Trump announced, via Truth Social: "VERY GOOD AND PRODUCTIVE CONVERSATIONS" with Tehran over a "COMPLETE AND TOTAL RESOLUTION" to hostilities.

Hours later, as has since become routine, Tehran refuted the claims and oil prices began climbing, sparking calls for an investigation into the trading.

"This appears abnormal, for sure," XAnalysts chief oil analyst Mukesh Sahdev told the BBC.

"At that time, there were no indications that any serious talks had been taking place between the US and Iran.

"So, to place so much money on oil going down raises questions."

Five months later, and the identity of those behind the trading remains a mystery.

America's corporate regulator, the Securities and Exchange Commission, has refused to confirm whether it has an active investigation underway, and it appears it has been left to the Department of Justice and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission.

The lack of action has stunned Democrats.

Back in April, New York congressman Ritchie Torres wrote to the SEC chair, Paul Atkins, imploring him to launch an immediate investigation.

"This occurrence may constitute one of the largest instances of insider trading in history," Torres wrote.

"Whether or not that ultimately proves to be the case, the seriousness of the allegations demands immediate transparency."

Trading off presidential statements already has gone beyond traditional financial markets, shifting to areas that allow trades on almost anything.

Push for prediction markets Kalshi and Polymarket have gone from obscure start-ups to two of the world's biggest prediction markets where users bet on yes-or-no questions spanning politics, pop culture and war.

In recent years, the rise of prediction markets like Polymarket and Kalshi has been used to bet on political and financial outcomes, raising concerns about the ethics of online betting and whether inside information is helping profiteers cash in on war.

A recent study by Columbia Law School and the University of Haifa has examined the blockchain ledger in search of odd trading patterns and discovered transactions generating profits of about $US143 million.

"The idea that someone would trade on national security information or information about upcoming terrorist activity — people thought that's not even possible," Joshua Mitts, a law professor at Columbia and one of the co-authors, told Bloomberg.

"Today what we're seeing in these prediction markets is that actually it is quite possible."

No more audits

In the past few days, Todd Blanche, the acting head of the US Department of Justice, finalised the incredible offer made to Donald Trump and members of his extended family last May on his tax position.

Under the arrangement, Trump cannot be audited or examined by the Internal Revenue Service for any year up until May this year.

Blanche, formerly the president's personal criminal defence lawyer, wound back some of the provisions in his earlier immunity offer, negotiated in exchange for Trump dropping his $US10 billion lawsuit against the IRS.

The acting head of the US Department of Justice, Todd Blanche, was formerly President Trump's personal lawyer. (Reuters: Ken Cedeno)

But with the substantive agreements remaining, the deal has far-reaching ramifications, given such immunity has never been applied to any president in history.

According to Liz Oyer, a former Department of Justice lawyer in charge of pardons and who was sacked earlier this year, the immunity deal is incredibly valuable to the president.

"Last year alone, Donald Trump made over $US2 billion," she told MS NOW (formerly MSNBC).

"There is nothing to make him pay his taxes on that money at this point."

Oyer estimates that the immunity agreement, in addition to letting him off the hook on any previous actions with the IRS, could excuse the president from paying hundreds of millions of dollars in tax on last year's earnings.

In the meantime, questions continue to be raised about the Trump family's business arrangements with the government.

The Washington Post this week published an expose on Department of Defence contracts awarded to companies in which Eric and Donald Trump Jr have an association.

These companies had seen government contracts and other funding arrangements grow to $US3.2 billion, a more-than-threefold increase since Trump's second term.

The Trump brothers claim their investments — many in new forms of warfare and weaponry — are a patriotic commitment to creating new American jobs and defeating China in the areas of drones and AI.

They have also stressed that they have never worked in government and are passive investors with no direct control over the companies.

But the president's personal and family business dealings stand in sharp contrast to those of his predecessors.

His most recent filings run to 927 pages and include 21,000 securities transactions and massive crypto ventures.

Joe Biden managed just 13 transactions in his entire four years in office.

World.title: Regional general store closing after larger competitors arrive
World.content:
After 102 years, the South West's historic Vasse General Store is closing its doors amid staunch retail competition in the growing residential area.

The century-old business has folded, with owners blaming the arrival of major supermarket, Coles and Vasse Farmers' Market, which is majority owned by Gina Rinehart's Hancock Prospecting.

The small business has suffered with big business capitalising on the town's booming population and road traffic generated by tourists travelling to popular locations throughout the region.

The store, originally founded by the McGuiness family in 1924 and located 232 kilometres south of Perth, has had just a handful of owners who each dedicated decades of their lives to taking very special care of the community keystone.

The Vasse General Store has operated for more than a century. (Supplied: Vasse General Store)

The price of progress

Gloria and Neil MacDonald took carriage of the store in 2000, working diligently to keep it afloat for 26 years, choosing to finally shut up shop and retire.

"I'll probably be a bit teary … but I know that I've done the best I can and it's been a great journey," Mrs MacDonald said.

On Saturday, the Vasse General Store hosted a closing celebration, commemorating 26 years of ownership by the MacDonalds and 102 years of operation. (Supplied: Vasse General Store)

The closure comes less than two years after nearby commercial developments were completed, landing Coles, McDonald's, Vasse Village and Shell on the small business's doorstep.

She said the recent explosion of major retailers just a few hundred metres away has impacted the business.

"People want to do a one-stop shop; they don't want to be traipsing around the town," Mrs MacDonald said.

Gloria and Neil MacDonald are set to retire after the store closes later this week. (Supplied: Vasse General Store)

She said the store still had a lot to offer that major supermarkets could not compete with.

"We got homemade cooking and … [supermarkets] don't fill the gap of the homemade cake," she said.

More than just a general store

For much of its life, the general store was one of a handful of businesses available to Vasse residents, acting as a fuel station, post office, shop and, most importantly, a place for community members to come together.

Mrs Macdonald said acting as a sounding board for customers has long been a part of her job description.

"Things might be rough in their world and they just need a shoulder to cry on and someone that's not going to be judgemental," she said.

" We'll go out the back and have a cup of tea and see if we can sort this out. "

Gloria MacDonald says her time at the store has been full of hard work and community connection. (Supplied: Vasse General Store)

Robert Harders sold the store to the MacDonalds in 2000, after running it with his wife Glenis for 17 years.

He said it was the people he connected with that stood out most when he reflected on his time at the store.

"It's the loyalty of the people that we dealt with,' Mr Harders said.

" They weren't [just] customers, they've become family. "

Robert Harders, with daughter Nerolee Warhurt, owned the Vasse General Store from 1983 to 2000. (ABC News: Georgia Loney)

A family affair

Mr Harders bought the general store in 1983, relocating his family of five from Perth to the South West, where he still lives today.

He said the store looked very different when he first set foot inside 43 years ago.

"[It had an] old wooden floor and they had the doors that picture-swing inwards and the wind used to whistle through," he said.

"They never had any debit cards or credit cards, so we used to run an account system.

"We made all the concrete on that where the fuel bows are and it still hasn't got any cracks in it so we must have done a pretty good job."

The concrete installed by the Harders Family remains at the Vasse General Store site today more than 40 years later. (Supplied)

Mr Harders's youngest daughter, Neisha Feutrill, had fond memories of her mother, who has since died, playing practical jokes in the shop.

"There's memories of her putting some pretty risque centrefolds in the milk delivery man's books," she said.

"So when he got to the next store, he opened it up and yeah, she had a really wicked sense of humour."

World.title: 7 million litres of diesel just 250m from homes: The data centre plan locals didn’t know about
World.content:
The former Ford car factory will become a $1.1 billion data centre campus, which would double Melbourne’s current data centre power draw when completed, under the government’s special fast-track major project approval process. The Campbellfield proposal has raised concerns about noise, pollution, fuel storage and its potentially fast-tracked government approval – as well as dashing hopes the site could once again become a major employment hub or a higher education campus in one of Melbourne’s most disadvantaged areas. Anastasia Drapaniotis says residents were not properly informed about the massive data centre proposal. Joe Armao Documents lodged with the state government show Singaporean-backed developer Zerra DC’s proposed “Project Dune” will consume 336 megawatts of power once fully operational across six stages. If built today, this would match the combined energy draw of all 55 operating data centres in Melbourne. The project, submitted directly to Planning Minister Sonya Kilkenny under special state planning provisions for big projects that bypass local councils and remove the option for residents to challenge them at the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal, spans 22 hectares at 300-340 Barry Road.



The data centre would take up roughly half of the total site between the Upfield train station and Sydney Road, which was home to the Ford car factory from 1959 until its closure in 2016. Stage one includes a two-storey, 48-megawatt data hall covering 30,000 square metres, supported by 48 emergency generators and 1 million litres of diesel fuel. The Ford Broadmeadows Assembly Plant, pictured when it was newly built in 1960, could become the site of a massive data centre. Gordon F. De'Lisle While the first stage is set back 650 metres from nearby houses, hazard and acoustic assessments confirm later stages will close the gap to just 260 metres from homes along Barry Road, and 290 metres from residential streets in Dallas. Subsequent stages will also sit 170 metres from homes and 130 metres from a medical centre and pathology clinic.



Anastasia Drapaniotis lives about 300 metres from where the centre would be built, and said most of her neighbours had no idea the development had been proposed and could be approved any day. The 30-year-old nurse said she received a vague notice in her letterbox last month on July 24 that said Zerra DC had lodged an application with the planning minister – just four days before the July 28 deadline after which Kilkenny could give it the green light. “The letter itself had little to no information about what this data centre actually was,” she said. “There’s a lot of elderly people, and they wouldn’t know how to go online to look this up. I went door-to-door to my neighbours, but they had no idea.”



The notice sent to residents in Campbellfield notifying them of Zerra DC’s proposed data centre, which included no information about the size or impact of the centre and gave them just days to respond. Drapaniotis said she was concerned about constant low-frequency noise the centre could produce, power supply, pollution from backup generators, and the fire risk from storing the equivalent of almost three Olympic swimming pools worth of diesel on site. “Heat islands” were another concern, she said, with recent University of Cambridge research showing new data centres warmed land around them by 2 degrees on average, and by up to 9 degrees in extreme cases. “In summer, we open up our windows at nighttime to let the cool breeze come in. With the noise, will we even be able to?” she asked. “It just shows that there is a lack of care and respect towards the community. They know how these centres will affect us, and they didn’t care to give us any more notice.”



While the facility would occupy an immense footprint – more than 10 times the size of the MCG’s playing surface – application reports reveal it will generate minimal long-term employment once built. Stage one will require 49 employees to operate, and this will grow to 255 on-site staff when all six stages are completed over a 12-year build, reports submitted as part of the planning application say. The Ford Broadmeadows Assembly Plant employed nearly 5200 people at its peak in the 1980s, mostly from migrant backgrounds and living in surrounding suburbs, and produced more than 600 cars a day. Since the end of the auto industry in Australia, Ford’s former chassis plant in Geelong has transformed into an advanced manufacturing hub with the help of significant federal and state support, while Victoria has committed $179 million to turn the former Holden site in Fishermans Bend into an “innovation precinct”. Hume councillor Naim Kurt was the local council’s appointee to the 2017 Broadmeadows Revitalisation Board, which considered future uses for the Campbellfield site, and said the community felt let down that there had not been the same level of government support to maximise employment opportunities there.



“A lot of promises were made about manufacturing continuing in the area and maximising employment,” Kurt said. “It was the largest undivided industrial block of land in the northern suburbs, in a strategic industrial precinct, and it needed to be kept together and used for the highest use of employment and continuance of manufacturing. And if not manufacturing, then education.” An artist’s impression of the proposed data centre on Barry Road, Campbellfield, on the site of what was once Ford’s manufacturing plant. Zerra DC Campbellfield and the neighbouring suburbs of Meadow Heights and Broadmeadows had twice the unemployment rate of the rest of the state at the last census of more than 10 per cent. Hume councillors will on Monday night consider a motion to call for a moratorium on new data centre approvals until the government develops a new framework to manage their environmental and economic impacts.



“The data centre could bring investment, create employment opportunities and support new technology and innovation,” Mayor Carly Moore said. “But there are significant concerns about whether it would deliver the lasting economic and community benefits we should expect from such an important site.” Broadmeadows state Labor MP Kathleen Matthews-Ward said she did not believe the site was suitable for a data centre, and had raised concerns about the proposal within government. “Given its manufacturing history and proximity to freeways, freight rail and the airports, I think this location would be best used for productive and advanced manufacturing,” she said. “I have also requested an improved consultation process on the project given the high proportion of local residents that do not speak English at home.” Zerra DC said the project would be a productive use of industrially zoned land which had the grid capacity and connectivity to support a data centre.



“The project will deliver an economic boost to the local community through construction activity, employment and local spending,” they said. “In further support of the local economy, we have incorporated a local supply and procurement requirement into the project, with a focus on prioritising local businesses, trades and materials where possible.” The vast former site of the Ford factory site, now destined to be the home for a new data centre. The Upfield railway line runs to the right of the site in this picture, and Sydney Road is on the left. In the distance is Melbourne’s city centre. Joe Armao Property developers Pelligra Group bought the Campbellfield site in 2019. Its chairman, Ross Pelligra, said Zerra DC would purchase around half the total site if its centre were approved, and he was working towards developing and leasing the remainder of the site with interest from manufacturing, logistics and food industries. A spokesperson for the planning minister said Kilkenny would consider the fast-tracked Development Facilitation Program application on its merits, with input from the local council, the Environment Protection Authority (EPA), Fire Rescue Victoria and the local electricity distribution and water authorities.



“Submissions from the community and nearby business can be provided up until a decision is made,” the spokesperson said. Zerra DC’s application outlines the first stage would be followed by three subsequent two-storey, 48-megawatt data halls ranging between 28,000 and 32,000 square metres. The final two stages will mark a step-change in height and capacity, introducing two three-storey, 72-megawatt halls measuring more than 44,000 square metres each. Due to the intense heat data servers generate, continuous cooling is vital. Zerra DC plans to use closed-loop air-cooled chillers to avoid drawing heavy volumes from Melbourne’s water supply. But reductions in water use come with a trade-off: greater energy use for cooling. So dramatic will the energy demand be to cool the hundreds of racks of servers inside the data centres that the project will ultimately house 294 rooftop chillers – 44 in stage one, and 250 in subsequent phases – alongside dozens of condensers and exhaust fans. Acoustic modelling by engineering firm Aurecon completed as part of the application found stage one’s 44 chillers would create a low-frequency hum that will fall within EPA guidelines.



But to handle the cumulative noise that will creep up under later stages – which will be built closer to homes – the developer will be forced to construct acoustic screening walls up to eight metres high on the roofs of stages two to six. World.title: Crockett, Bullock eye sprint success with in-form mare
World.content:
SportRacingHorse racing Crockett, Bullock eye sprint success with in-form mare Neil Evans August 9, 2026 — 5:33pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

One of the state’s most potent trainer-jockey combinations rejoin forces to hunt another sprint scalp at Monday’s feature Dubbo meeting. On Dubbo Cup and Sprint Prelude day, Scone-based Cameron Crockett and top jockey Aaron Bullock combine aboard a tough and ultra-consistent mare chasing a third straight win in the feature dash over 1120m. Top jockey Aaron Bullock will take the reins on Not Written Off on Monday. Getty Images Not Written Off, a still lightly raced six-year-old daughter of Written By, has taken her strike rate to nearly 30 per cent from 23 starts by winning her last couple at Tamworth. She drove home very late to claim a Benchmark 74, before an even more impressive win when finishing hard in a BM 82.



Now, two big factors suggest she’s again ripe for the money at Dubbo. Not only has Bullock been booked to ride, the stable elected to run promising and resuming stablemate Where’stheprofit at Sunday’s Muswellbrook card instead. Crockett is easily in the best run of his career. Before that closer at Muswellbrook, he had a terrific 10 individual winners from his last 16 runners, including consecutive Class 3 Highways at Randwick with Leovanni, and the feature Kirby sprint at Grafton with Durova. Bullock too is not taking his foot off the pedal.



A treble at last Friday’s Coffs Harbour meeting took his winning haul to nine from his last 26 rides, and 17 from his last 50. Related Article Horse racing Tips and race-by-race guide for Dubbo on Monday Not Written Off opened around $4 in early betting for the Sprint Prelude, but is destined to start much shorter. Meanwhile, the Dubbo Cup Prelude over 1420m to close the meeting has Bullock teaming up with Inverell trainer Todd Payne aboard tough six-year-old Shamedy. Despite not having won since Armidale early last spring, Shamedy opened around $5.50 in a wide betting race just behind Prince Of Sorts ($5.00), with Nomorenightshift ($6.00) also well in commission.



The meeting is likely to be run on a soft surface, with showers forecast in the 24 hours leading up. Supplied by Racing NSW

World.title: ‘I’m sorry’: Father of Thailand’s school shooter offers first words
World.content:
WorldAsiaMass shooting ‘I’m sorry’: Father of Thailand’s school shooter offers first words Harry Jiaravongtrakul Zach Hope and August 9, 2026 — 5:15pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Bang Kruai District, Thailand: On Friday morning, Nanchanatporn Nakplang got up, made breakfast and went to work as usual at Debsirin Nonthaburi School. She had been a teacher for eight years and attended the school herself as a girl. By 10am, she was dead, killed by a 14-year-old gunman in a mass shooting that has rocked Thailand. The following afternoon, her body was laid out in a nearby Buddhist temple, where hundreds of mourners lined up to take holy water from a receptacle beside her. They were fellow teachers, neighbours, students and alumni. Teenagers and adults wept. A mourner prays and weeps over the body of teacher Nanchanatporn Nakplang. Zach Hope “This was a teacher who was loved by her students,” said Chawinthon Udomchaidate, an 18-year-old former student who had Kanun, as she was nicknamed, for Thai language lessons.



Kanun, in her early 30s, was one of five teachers killed at Debsirin Nonthaburi School, on the north-western fringes of Bangkok, in Thailand’s worst mass shooting since 2022. The school announced on Saturday afternoon, shortly after Kanun’s funeral service, that year 7 girl Naphat Chaima had also succumbed to her wounds in hospital. Nanchanatporn Nakplang was one of five teachers killed in Friday’s school shooting on the outskirts of Bangkok. Facebook The shooter was year 9 student Patchata Yimruang, who, relatives told Thai media, liked to keep to himself and spent his spare time playing video games. His father emerged from the nearby Plai Bang Police Station after an interview with investigators on Sunday. Fighting through the crowd of journalists and cameramen to get to his car, he offered only a couple of words in Thai.



“I’m sorry,” he said. Thailand has high gun ownership rates and a recent history of mass shootings, but not in schools or by students. The Thai shooter’s father, in white, leaving the police station on Sunday. Zach Hope The Debsirin Nonthaburi School shooting may prove Thailand’s Port Arthur moment, with Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul pledging to review the nation’s gun laws. Yimruang’s shooting spree began at home before dawn on Friday when he fatally shot his grandfather in the back and his grandmother while she was still in bed. He had lived with them since the age of two after his parents’ separation.



Related Article Graphic content

Mass shooting Teen gunman watched violent videos before killing seven in shooting rampage Locking the door behind him, Yimruang arrived at school at 6.20am as usual and participated in the flag-raising assembly. Shortly before 10am, as the second school period drew to a close, he produced from his bag the same 9mm handgun he had used to kill his grandparents and opened fire. Yimruang moved through the hallways shooting at teachers and students before turning the gun on himself as police formed a cordon around the multi-storey building’s perimeter. In addition to the dead, close to 30 people were injured, including students, in the gunfire or frantic escape that had some hiding on ledges outside upper-floor windows.



Police later found a drawing of a gun at the boy’s home and evidence on his computer that he had been watching online videos of mass shootings from America. It has also emerged that Yimruang last year brought a BB gun to school, for which he was disciplined. Loading Police still do not have a motive, although they have speculated that he had been under pressure from his grandparents and teachers about his school performance.



Police Major General Atthaporn Anusit spoke to reporters on Sunday at Plai Bang Police Station, but had little to offer the press pack. Related Article Tragedy Barricading doors, hiding under tables: Students tell of fleeing mass shooting at their Thai school “After investigation and interrogation with various people, we believe there are many related factors combined,” he said. “I want to pass on the message to anyone taking care of the youth: We must listen to them. Focus on problem-solving. Sometimes we may ignore them, but now with social media, they can access content on their own … we have to keep a closer look on the youth.” Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Knights shrug off loss of two more stars to sink Raiders’ finals hopes
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 Knights shrug off loss of two more stars to sink Raiders’ finals hopes August 9, 2026 — 5:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Newcastle have overcome the loss of key personnel to virtually end Canberra’s finals hopes by grinding out a see-sawing 30-24 victory at GIO Stadium. The Knights’ injury list ballooned before Sunday’s damp clash with centre Bradman Best and hooker Phoenix Crossland (both calf) ruled out, joining halfback Dylan Brown and second-rower Dylan Lucas on the sidelines. Loading But Newcastle (13-8), buoyed by celebrating Tyson Frizell’s 300th game, produced a fearless performance to solidify their position inside the top eight. The Knights may have more players to add to their casualty ward though, as Frizell hobbled off the field in the second half.



With the top four also in their sights, Justin Holbrook’s men are one step closer to completing a remarkable rebound after finishing with the wooden spoon last season. While Newcastle flirt with a finals berth, the Raiders’ ambitions of playing finals footy have been effectively ended as they can no longer secure a winning record. Newcastle winger Dom Young scored two tries on his 25th birthday. Getty Images Unless a mathematical miracle occurs, Canberra (9-12) will become the first team since the Sydney Roosters in 2016 to miss out on finals the year after claiming the minor premiership, as they sit six points adrift of eighth-placed North Queensland. The Green Machine’s loss was all but confirmed when Knights centre Dane Gagai was penalised with less than 10 minutes remaining metres from their own line, but the bunker overturned the decision because forward Corey Horsburgh struck Gagai.



With Newcastle ahead 26-24, Horsburgh was sent to the sin bin and minutes later Dom Young, on his 25th birthday, crossed for his second in the right corner to seal the victory. Related Article Opinion

NRL 2026 The audacious idea to play more matches in NRL grand final week Danny Weidler Sport columnist Despite Newcastle scoring the first two tries, Raiders winger Jed Stuart intercepted a looping Kalyn Ponga pass and ran 70 metres in the 17th minute before Zac Hosking snuck over to level the contest. The Knights hit back when Young tore down the right flank and gave the ball to a running Ponga. Centre Simi Sasagi crossed twice while battling through a suspected arm injury either side of halftime to take the lead for the home team.



But Gagai capitalised on a blistering Young run, before the winger completed the victory in the 78th minute. AAP

World.title: Unions, BHP urged to ‘nut out the detail’ as strike action enters second day
World.content:
NationalWAIron ore Unions, BHP urged to ‘nut out the detail’ as strike action enters second day Michael Philipps August 9, 2026 — 4:48pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Union representatives have called strikes at WA’s largest bulk export port as “significant” and urged a fast resolution as industrial action continued into a second day in the state’s Pilbara region. However, the miner says iron ore export vessels continue to be loaded and departures remain scheduled subject to usual port planning and tides. BHP says iron ore export ships continue to be loaded despite the ongoing strike action. The two-day industrial action began on Saturday with a 24-hour ship-loading ban and continued with a 24-hour work stoppage from 5.30am on Sunday. The strike involves workers from the Combined Ports Unions, made up of members from the Electrical Trades Union, the Australian Manufacturing Workers’ Union and the Western Mine Workers Alliance, and follows action that saw members stop work for an eight-hour period last month.



AWU WA assistant secretary Craig Beveridge said BHP had continually refused to negotiate in good faith. Related Article Mining Why workers earning $200,000 a year are getting ready to walk off the job “These actions are a direct message to the company that all union members are standing together in solidarity,” he said “They are strong, and they are prepared to take whatever action is necessary to secure an enterprise agreement that is acceptable to the workforce.” A BHP spokesperson said that with around 1200 people on site across its port facility, the company’s priority is continuing safe and productive operations.



“Vessels are continuing to be loaded with scheduled departures subject to usual port planning and tides,” the spokesperson said. “Our focus remains on reaching a fair and reasonable agreement. Our approach will deliver greater pay consistency across the workforce while locking in industry leading pay and conditions.” Beveridge said union members also remain committed to good faith negotiations when they next meet BHP on August 18. “But BHP must understand that the days of ignoring the legitimate claims of their workforce are over,” he said. “We are seeking an agreement that addresses the log of claims presented by employees at the beginning of this process.



“Our members know the impact of them withdrawing their labour at Port Hedland over this weekend was significant and BHP knows the impact of our members withdrawing their labour this weekend was significant. “Our hope is that this protected industrial action does exactly what it’s intended to do, which is sharpen all parties’ minds on finding a solution that works for everyone fast. “BHP must understand that the Combined Ports Unions will not be deterred by threats or intimidation.” An AWU spokesman said BHP management recently issued written communication threatening that any worker who participates in planned bans on ship loading activities would face the deduction of a full day’s pay, regardless of how many hours they worked on other essential tasks during their shift. However, a BHP spokesperson rejected those claims.



“Workplace laws are clear that we are not required to pay for the portion of an employee’s work that is subject to an industrial ban,” the BHP spokesperson said. “Unfortunately, with the additional 47 work activities the AWU advised us would be subject to their bans, there was no productive work left that the small number of employees who chose to take industrial action could undertake, and therefore no reason for them to attend work.” WA Industrial Relations Minister Simone McGurk urged both parties to continue to meet to “nut out the fine detail”. “If there’s a bit of give and take on both sides, I’m sure agreement could be reached,” she said.

World.title: Bowled out for 54 in their warm-up game, can Bangladesh avoid Test match humiliation?
World.content:
SportCricketAustralian cricket Bowled out for 54 in their warm-up game, can Bangladesh avoid Test match humiliation? Daniel Brettig August 9, 2026 — 4:46pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Darwin: Bangladesh will need to channel some of the unbridled aggression of their injured spearhead Nahid Rana if they wish to avoid Test match humiliation by Australia after being knocked over for 54 in their sole warm-up game. Before he maddeningly tore a side in a series against Zimbabwe from which other members of the Test squad were rested, 23-year-old Rana was breathing fire ahead of Bangladesh’s first two Tests in Australia since 2003. Bangladesh’s Nahid Rana was a key performer in the ODI series win over Australia but won’t take part in the Test series in Australia. AP Photo He was a key to their victory over Australia on home soil in a recent ODI series, notably getting into a confrontation with acting captain and Test squad member Josh Inglis that underlined his desire not to take a backward step. “If someone shows me respect on the field, I will show them respect as a fellow professional,” Rana told this masthead before his injury. “It is a case of mutual appreciation for the job we are doing, and I understand that sometimes words will be exchanged.



“However, if I feel that the line has been crossed through words or actions on the field, I will try to return the favour using my strengths. Related Article Opinion

Test cricket Australia will play a Test cricket series against Bangladesh in the footy season. This is not good Malcolm Knox Journalist, author and columnist “Normally, if someone says something to me off the field, I would probably ignore it and walk away. But when I am inside the ground representing my country, it is a completely different story. I am not there to make friends.” By contrast, the touring team was meekness personified in being rolled for just 54 by a Cricket Australia Invitational team, led by young South Australian left-armer Campbell Thompson, who scooped 8-25 with accurate lines and a hint of swing. “To clean it up this morning, I had a clear process – just try to use the new ball, swing it and hit the stumps – and I was lucky enough to get a few wickets,” Thompson said after his haul.



“The length we had to bowl in the second innings was probably a bit shorter than in the first innings – so just dragging it back a bit, hitting the top of the stumps, and clear processes was the main goal. “I feel like I’m a new-ball bowler, so I’m just trying to swing the ball and hit the stumps, and I got lucky this time.” Australia v Bangladesh Test series First Test: From August 13-17 at TIO Stadium in Darwin Second Test: From August 22-26 at Great Barrier Reef Arena in Mackay Australian squad: Pat Cummins (c), Scott Boland, Alex Carey, Cameron Green , Josh Hazlewood, Travis Head, Josh Inglis, Marnus Labuschagne, Nathan Lyon, Steve Smith, Mitchell Starc, Jake Weatherald, Beau Webster. While the swift end to the game was great for Thompson and his teammates, it augured badly for this week's first of two Tests between Bangladesh and Australia's heavy duty team, fronted by Pat Cummins, Mitchell Starc and company. Before the 2003 series, the late David Hookes set tongues wagging by suggesting that the team led by Steve Waugh should try to beat the visitors in a single day’s play.



“Steve Waugh should send them in to bat, bowl them out before lunch, bat until tea and declare, then send them back in and roll them again before stumps,” Hookes had said. “It could be all over and done within a day. “The reality is that Bangladesh doesn’t deserve to be in Test cricket, and they certainly shouldn’t be given any favours out on the field. If the Australian team is being true to the Test cap, their aim will be go to out there and annihilate Bangladesh.” Loading As it turned out, Bangladesh lost both those Tests by an innings, but the games in Darwin and Cairns lasted for three and four days respectively. Since then, Bangladesh have made great strides as a cricket nation, in no small part due to the aid of numerous Australian coaches, from Jamie Siddons and Shane Jurgensen to Shaun Tait.



Their ODI series victory over Australia was notable for taking place on a trip of excellent pitches, which had good pace and bounce for the quicks, while good stroke play was rewarded. Related Article Exclusive

Australian cricket ‘They hid it away’: The DNA test that revealed an Australian cricketer’s family secret But those heady moments looked a long way away on Saturday as Thompson ran through a timid touring side – about as far away as Rana, resting up back home after an injury that has robbed the series of its most likely fireworks. Also absent for Bangladesh is Mustafizur Rahman, who now concentrates on white-ball formats and, if not for injury, would be playing in the Hundred in the UK. It will now be up to the likes of Taskin Ahmed to ask questions of Australia’s batting. “He is the quiet type in the dressing room, but the way he goes about his business, his professionalism, his intelligence and his ability to execute his skills relentlessly year after year is fascinating and extraordinary,” Rana said of the man known as “The Fizz”.



“Apart from the Fizz, I talk to my seniors in the fast-bowling department all the time. They had started the pace revolution for Bangladesh before I came in ... we are like a band of brothers.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: ‘We’ve been waiting for years’: Plenty of buzz as Metro completion approaches
World.content:
PoliticsNSWSydney Metro ‘We’ve been waiting for years’: Plenty of buzz as Metro completion approaches Michael McGowan August 9, 2026 — 4:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Welcome to Metro in the ’burbs. Almost two years after it closed, along with nine other stations along the south-west corridor as part of the tricky final 13-kilometre completion of the M1 Metro line, Dulwich Hill looks … well, pretty much the same. South Marrickville resident Sophie Duxson, right, with friend Olivia Rosenman and Sol, 3, and Aspasia, 6. Sitthixay Ditthavong But if the reaction from the hundreds of Metro-heads who turned up to a community open day at the soon-to-reopen station on Sunday is anything to go by, people won’t mind once the trains start running. As with most commuters along the west and south-west corridor, Sophie Duxson, from South Marrickville, is well and truly ready to see the end of the pink replacement buses that have ferried passengers between Sydenham and Bankstown since the line closed in September 2024.



Duxson commutes to the city and Parramatta for work, and the latter trip has been taking her about an hour-and-a-half since the line closed, with a bus to Petersham and then all-stops train to Parramatta. She, like the roughly 9500 passengers expected to catch the trains during the morning peak of 8 to 9am, is ready for it to end. “We’ve been waiting for years,” she said. “Look, the buses have actually been really well managed and everyone loves our local Metro lady at this stop. She is so lovely. She feeds everyone’s dogs. They’ve been some of the best rail replacement buses I’ve dealt with, to be honest. But we’re still over it. It’s been almost two years.” Summer Hill MP Jo Haylen attends a community open day at Dulwich Hill station with her family. Sitthixay Ditthavong Glittering architectural designs stunned Sydneysiders when the CBD stations opened in 2024, but Metro Project Director Alia Karaman said commuters on the south-west extension should not expect to find “cathedrals” when the stations re-open in the coming months.



Beyond the addition of the by-now familiar Metro doors and fresh paint, those touring the new station on Sunday won’t have seen much that wasn’t there before. Looks can be deceiving, however. Karaman said Dulwich Hill was one of the most challenging stations during the line conversion, in part due to the curved tracks leading into and out of the platform, as well as its position along the freight rail line. Some stations have undergone more significant change. The new Bankstown plaza is a major addition to that station, for example. At the same time, heritage buildings and concourses at Dulwich Hill and other stations have been refreshed and renewed, and acting Metro chief executive Hugh Lawson said maintaining the feel and functionality of suburban stations had been important. “They are what people need. They’re in the right setting. The community wanted to retain the heritage features so we’ve worked hard to do that,” he said. When the Sydney metro extension through the CBD opened it was justifiably hailed as a transformative piece of infrastructure. It sparked a wave of excitement – from bar crawls to food tours – as Sydney residents took advantage of newly convenient access to parts of the city previously seen as prohibitively distant.



Jo Haylen, the MP for Summer Hill, said the extension from Sydenham to Bankstown would only add to that excitement. “We already saw people taking food tours on the city Metro. Wait until we open south-west,” she said. “You’ll be able to jump on at Vic Square [in North Sydney] and have dinner in Lakemba or Punchbowl.” Most important, though, would be the ease of transport for residents along the line. “I think people have been thankful [the pink buses] have been free and frequent but, particularly getting through this winter, I know how tight some of those cold mornings have been. I think they’ll be happy to see the back of them. It’ll be so much easier to just turn up here and go,” she said. “We’re going to be in the city in the flash of an eye. It’s going to be incredible. I’m excited. My kids are excited.”



The government has refused to say when the new line will open, though a mid-October opening appears likely. The line is in final stages of testing, which includes emergency training scenarios with Police and Fire and Rescue. Be the first to know when major news happens.

World.title: 7 million litres of diesel just 250m from homes: The data centre plan locals didn’t know about
World.content:
The former Ford car factory will become a $1.1 billion data centre campus, which would double Melbourne’s current data centre power draw when completed, under the government’s special fast-track major project approval process. The Campbellfield proposal has raised concerns about noise, pollution, fuel storage and its potentially fast-tracked government approval – as well as dashing hopes the site could once again become a major employment hub or a higher education campus in one of Melbourne’s most disadvantaged areas. Anastasia Drapaniotis says residents were not properly informed about the massive data centre proposal. Joe Armao Documents lodged with the state government show Singaporean-backed developer Zerra DC’s proposed “Project Dune” will consume 336 megawatts of power once fully operational across six stages. If built today, this would match the combined energy draw of all 55 operating data centres in Melbourne. The project, submitted directly to Planning Minister Sonya Kilkenny under special state planning provisions for big projects that bypass local councils and remove the option for residents to challenge them at the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal, spans 22 hectares at 300-340 Barry Road.



The data centre would take up roughly half of the total site between the Upfield train station and Sydney Road, which was home to the Ford car factory from 1959 until its closure in 2016. Stage one includes a two-storey, 48-megawatt data hall covering 30,000 square metres, supported by 48 emergency generators and 1 million litres of diesel fuel. The Ford Broadmeadows Assembly Plant, pictured when it was newly built in 1960, could become the site of a massive data centre. Gordon F. De'Lisle While the first stage is set back 650 metres from nearby houses, hazard and acoustic assessments confirm later stages will close the gap to just 260 metres from homes along Barry Road, and 290 metres from residential streets in Dallas. Subsequent stages will also sit 170 metres from homes and 130 metres from a medical centre and pathology clinic.



Anastasia Drapaniotis lives about 300 metres from where the centre would be built, and said most of her neighbours had no idea the development had been proposed and could be approved any day. The 30-year-old nurse said she received a vague notice in her letterbox last month on July 24 that said Zerra DC had lodged an application with the planning minister – just four days before the July 28 deadline after which Kilkenny could give it the green light. “The letter itself had little to no information about what this data centre actually was,” she said. “There’s a lot of elderly people, and they wouldn’t know how to go online to look this up. I went door-to-door to my neighbours, but they had no idea.”



The notice sent to residents in Campbellfield notifying them of Zerra DC’s proposed data centre, which included no information about the size or impact of the centre and gave them just days to respond. Drapaniotis said she was concerned about constant low-frequency noise the centre could produce, power supply, pollution from backup generators, and the fire risk from storing the equivalent of almost three Olympic swimming pools worth of diesel on site. “Heat islands” were another concern, she said, with recent University of Cambridge research showing new data centres warmed land around them by 2 degrees on average, and by up to 9 degrees in extreme cases. “In summer, we open up our windows at nighttime to let the cool breeze come in. With the noise, will we even be able to?” she asked. “It just shows that there is a lack of care and respect towards the community. They know how these centres will affect us, and they didn’t care to give us any more notice.”



While the facility would occupy an immense footprint – more than 10 times the size of the MCG’s playing surface – application reports reveal it will generate minimal long-term employment once built. Stage one will require 49 employees to operate, and this will grow to 255 on-site staff when all six stages are completed over a 12-year build, reports submitted as part of the planning application say. The Ford Broadmeadows Assembly Plant employed nearly 5200 people at its peak in the 1980s, mostly from migrant backgrounds and living in surrounding suburbs, and produced more than 600 cars a day. Since the end of the auto industry in Australia, Ford’s former chassis plant in Geelong has transformed into an advanced manufacturing hub with the help of significant federal and state support, while Victoria has committed $179 million to turn the former Holden site in Fishermans Bend into an “innovation precinct”. Hume councillor Naim Kurt was the local council’s appointee to the 2017 Broadmeadows Revitalisation Board, which considered future uses for the Campbellfield site, and said the community felt let down that there had not been the same level of government support to maximise employment opportunities there.



“A lot of promises were made about manufacturing continuing in the area and maximising employment,” Kurt said. “It was the largest undivided industrial block of land in the northern suburbs, in a strategic industrial precinct, and it needed to be kept together and used for the highest use of employment and continuance of manufacturing. And if not manufacturing, then education.” An artist’s impression of the proposed data centre on Barry Road, Campbellfield, on the site of what was once Ford’s manufacturing plant. Zerra DC Campbellfield and the neighbouring suburbs of Meadow Heights and Broadmeadows had twice the unemployment rate of the rest of the state at the last census of more than 10 per cent. Hume councillors will on Monday night consider a motion to call for a moratorium on new data centre approvals until the government develops a new framework to manage their environmental and economic impacts.



“The data centre could bring investment, create employment opportunities and support new technology and innovation,” Mayor Carly Moore said. “But there are significant concerns about whether it would deliver the lasting economic and community benefits we should expect from such an important site.” Broadmeadows state Labor MP Kathleen Matthews-Ward said she did not believe the site was suitable for a data centre, and had raised concerns about the proposal within government. “Given its manufacturing history and proximity to freeways, freight rail and the airports, I think this location would be best used for productive and advanced manufacturing,” she said. “I have also requested an improved consultation process on the project given the high proportion of local residents that do not speak English at home.” Zerra DC said the project would be a productive use of industrially zoned land which had the grid capacity and connectivity to support a data centre.



“The project will deliver an economic boost to the local community through construction activity, employment and local spending,” they said. “In further support of the local economy, we have incorporated a local supply and procurement requirement into the project, with a focus on prioritising local businesses, trades and materials where possible.” The vast former site of the Ford factory site, now destined to be the home for a new data centre. The Upfield railway line runs to the right of the site in this picture, and Sydney Road is on the left. In the distance is Melbourne’s city centre. Joe Armao Property developers Pelligra Group bought the Campbellfield site in 2019. Its chairman, Ross Pelligra, said Zerra DC would purchase around half the total site if its centre were approved, and he was working towards developing and leasing the remainder of the site with interest from manufacturing, logistics and food industries. A spokesperson for the planning minister said Kilkenny would consider the fast-tracked Development Facilitation Program application on its merits, with input from the local council, the Environment Protection Authority (EPA), Fire Rescue Victoria and the local electricity distribution and water authorities.



“Submissions from the community and nearby business can be provided up until a decision is made,” the spokesperson said. Zerra DC’s application outlines the first stage would be followed by three subsequent two-storey, 48-megawatt data halls ranging between 28,000 and 32,000 square metres. The final two stages will mark a step-change in height and capacity, introducing two three-storey, 72-megawatt halls measuring more than 44,000 square metres each. Due to the intense heat data servers generate, continuous cooling is vital. Zerra DC plans to use closed-loop air-cooled chillers to avoid drawing heavy volumes from Melbourne’s water supply. But reductions in water use come with a trade-off: greater energy use for cooling. So dramatic will the energy demand be to cool the hundreds of racks of servers inside the data centres that the project will ultimately house 294 rooftop chillers – 44 in stage one, and 250 in subsequent phases – alongside dozens of condensers and exhaust fans. Acoustic modelling by engineering firm Aurecon completed as part of the application found stage one’s 44 chillers would create a low-frequency hum that will fall within EPA guidelines.



But to handle the cumulative noise that will creep up under later stages – which will be built closer to homes – the developer will be forced to construct acoustic screening walls up to eight metres high on the roofs of stages two to six. World.title: Crockett, Bullock eye sprint success with in-form mare
World.content:
SportRacingHorse racing Crockett, Bullock eye sprint success with in-form mare Neil Evans August 9, 2026 — 5:33pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

One of the state’s most potent trainer-jockey combinations rejoin forces to hunt another sprint scalp at Monday’s feature Dubbo meeting. On Dubbo Cup and Sprint Prelude day, Scone-based Cameron Crockett and top jockey Aaron Bullock combine aboard a tough and ultra-consistent mare chasing a third straight win in the feature dash over 1120m. Top jockey Aaron Bullock will take the reins on Not Written Off on Monday. Getty Images Not Written Off, a still lightly raced six-year-old daughter of Written By, has taken her strike rate to nearly 30 per cent from 23 starts by winning her last couple at Tamworth. She drove home very late to claim a Benchmark 74, before an even more impressive win when finishing hard in a BM 82.



Now, two big factors suggest she’s again ripe for the money at Dubbo. Not only has Bullock been booked to ride, the stable elected to run promising and resuming stablemate Where’stheprofit at Sunday’s Muswellbrook card instead. Crockett is easily in the best run of his career. Before that closer at Muswellbrook, he had a terrific 10 individual winners from his last 16 runners, including consecutive Class 3 Highways at Randwick with Leovanni, and the feature Kirby sprint at Grafton with Durova. Bullock too is not taking his foot off the pedal.



A treble at last Friday’s Coffs Harbour meeting took his winning haul to nine from his last 26 rides, and 17 from his last 50. Related Article Horse racing Tips and race-by-race guide for Dubbo on Monday Not Written Off opened around $4 in early betting for the Sprint Prelude, but is destined to start much shorter. Meanwhile, the Dubbo Cup Prelude over 1420m to close the meeting has Bullock teaming up with Inverell trainer Todd Payne aboard tough six-year-old Shamedy. Despite not having won since Armidale early last spring, Shamedy opened around $5.50 in a wide betting race just behind Prince Of Sorts ($5.00), with Nomorenightshift ($6.00) also well in commission.



The meeting is likely to be run on a soft surface, with showers forecast in the 24 hours leading up. Supplied by Racing NSW

Further boosted with two early rivals, including the talented stablemate, being preferred at Muswellbrook on Sunday. 1. Vendor has hit the line nicely in his last couple.

How to play it: De Joker to win. Race 7

Prince Of Sorts drew wide under a big weight third-up, but impressed when close up in a BM 68 at Wyong. 6. Hibiki Harmony did her best work late when resuming in a feature BM 87 at Muswellbrook. 10. Navy Steel can improve sharply second-up after being tailed off in a deeper metro race, while 11. World.title: ‘I’m sorry’: Father of Thailand’s school shooter offers first words
World.content:
WorldAsiaMass shooting ‘I’m sorry’: Father of Thailand’s school shooter offers first words Harry Jiaravongtrakul Zach Hope and August 9, 2026 — 5:15pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Bang Kruai District, Thailand: On Friday morning, Nanchanatporn Nakplang got up, made breakfast and went to work as usual at Debsirin Nonthaburi School. She had been a teacher for eight years and attended the school herself as a girl. By 10am, she was dead, killed by a 14-year-old gunman in a mass shooting that has rocked Thailand. The following afternoon, her body was laid out in a nearby Buddhist temple, where hundreds of mourners lined up to take holy water from a receptacle beside her. They were fellow teachers, neighbours, students and alumni. Teenagers and adults wept. A mourner prays and weeps over the body of teacher Nanchanatporn Nakplang. Zach Hope “This was a teacher who was loved by her students,” said Chawinthon Udomchaidate, an 18-year-old former student who had Kanun, as she was nicknamed, for Thai language lessons.



Kanun, in her early 30s, was one of five teachers killed at Debsirin Nonthaburi School, on the north-western fringes of Bangkok, in Thailand’s worst mass shooting since 2022. The school announced on Saturday afternoon, shortly after Kanun’s funeral service, that year 7 girl Naphat Chaima had also succumbed to her wounds in hospital. Nanchanatporn Nakplang was one of five teachers killed in Friday’s school shooting on the outskirts of Bangkok. Facebook The shooter was year 9 student Patchata Yimruang, who, relatives told Thai media, liked to keep to himself and spent his spare time playing video games. His father emerged from the nearby Plai Bang Police Station after an interview with investigators on Sunday. Fighting through the crowd of journalists and cameramen to get to his car, he offered only a couple of words in Thai.



“I’m sorry,” he said. Thailand has high gun ownership rates and a recent history of mass shootings, but not in schools or by students. The Thai shooter’s father, in white, leaving the police station on Sunday. Zach Hope The Debsirin Nonthaburi School shooting may prove Thailand’s Port Arthur moment, with Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul pledging to review the nation’s gun laws. Yimruang’s shooting spree began at home before dawn on Friday when he fatally shot his grandfather in the back and his grandmother while she was still in bed. He had lived with them since the age of two after his parents’ separation.



Related Article Graphic content

Mass shooting Teen gunman watched violent videos before killing seven in shooting rampage Locking the door behind him, Yimruang arrived at school at 6.20am as usual and participated in the flag-raising assembly. Shortly before 10am, as the second school period drew to a close, he produced from his bag the same 9mm handgun he had used to kill his grandparents and opened fire. Yimruang moved through the hallways shooting at teachers and students before turning the gun on himself as police formed a cordon around the multi-storey building’s perimeter. In addition to the dead, close to 30 people were injured, including students, in the gunfire or frantic escape that had some hiding on ledges outside upper-floor windows.



Police later found a drawing of a gun at the boy’s home and evidence on his computer that he had been watching online videos of mass shootings from America. It has also emerged that Yimruang last year brought a BB gun to school, for which he was disciplined. Loading Police still do not have a motive, although they have speculated that he had been under pressure from his grandparents and teachers about his school performance.



Police Major General Atthaporn Anusit spoke to reporters on Sunday at Plai Bang Police Station, but had little to offer the press pack. Related Article Tragedy Barricading doors, hiding under tables: Students tell of fleeing mass shooting at their Thai school “After investigation and interrogation with various people, we believe there are many related factors combined,” he said. “I want to pass on the message to anyone taking care of the youth: We must listen to them. Focus on problem-solving. Sometimes we may ignore them, but now with social media, they can access content on their own … we have to keep a closer look on the youth.” Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Knights shrug off loss of two more stars to sink Raiders’ finals hopes
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 Knights shrug off loss of two more stars to sink Raiders’ finals hopes August 9, 2026 — 5:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Newcastle have overcome the loss of key personnel to virtually end Canberra’s finals hopes by grinding out a see-sawing 30-24 victory at GIO Stadium. The Knights’ injury list ballooned before Sunday’s damp clash with centre Bradman Best and hooker Phoenix Crossland (both calf) ruled out, joining halfback Dylan Brown and second-rower Dylan Lucas on the sidelines. Loading But Newcastle (13-8), buoyed by celebrating Tyson Frizell’s 300th game, produced a fearless performance to solidify their position inside the top eight. The Knights may have more players to add to their casualty ward though, as Frizell hobbled off the field in the second half.



With the top four also in their sights, Justin Holbrook’s men are one step closer to completing a remarkable rebound after finishing with the wooden spoon last season. While Newcastle flirt with a finals berth, the Raiders’ ambitions of playing finals footy have been effectively ended as they can no longer secure a winning record. Newcastle winger Dom Young scored two tries on his 25th birthday. Getty Images Unless a mathematical miracle occurs, Canberra (9-12) will become the first team since the Sydney Roosters in 2016 to miss out on finals the year after claiming the minor premiership, as they sit six points adrift of eighth-placed North Queensland. The Green Machine’s loss was all but confirmed when Knights centre Dane Gagai was penalised with less than 10 minutes remaining metres from their own line, but the bunker overturned the decision because forward Corey Horsburgh struck Gagai.



With Newcastle ahead 26-24, Horsburgh was sent to the sin bin and minutes later Dom Young, on his 25th birthday, crossed for his second in the right corner to seal the victory. Related Article Opinion

NRL 2026 The audacious idea to play more matches in NRL grand final week Danny Weidler Sport columnist Despite Newcastle scoring the first two tries, Raiders winger Jed Stuart intercepted a looping Kalyn Ponga pass and ran 70 metres in the 17th minute before Zac Hosking snuck over to level the contest. The Knights hit back when Young tore down the right flank and gave the ball to a running Ponga. Centre Simi Sasagi crossed twice while battling through a suspected arm injury either side of halftime to take the lead for the home team.



But Gagai capitalised on a blistering Young run, before the winger completed the victory in the 78th minute. AAP

World.title: Unions, BHP urged to ‘nut out the detail’ as strike action enters second day
World.content:
NationalWAIron ore Unions, BHP urged to ‘nut out the detail’ as strike action enters second day Michael Philipps August 9, 2026 — 4:48pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Union representatives have called strikes at WA’s largest bulk export port as “significant” and urged a fast resolution as industrial action continued into a second day in the state’s Pilbara region. However, the miner says iron ore export vessels continue to be loaded and departures remain scheduled subject to usual port planning and tides. BHP says iron ore export ships continue to be loaded despite the ongoing strike action. The two-day industrial action began on Saturday with a 24-hour ship-loading ban and continued with a 24-hour work stoppage from 5.30am on Sunday. The strike involves workers from the Combined Ports Unions, made up of members from the Electrical Trades Union, the Australian Manufacturing Workers’ Union and the Western Mine Workers Alliance, and follows action that saw members stop work for an eight-hour period last month.



AWU WA assistant secretary Craig Beveridge said BHP had continually refused to negotiate in good faith. Related Article Mining Why workers earning $200,000 a year are getting ready to walk off the job “These actions are a direct message to the company that all union members are standing together in solidarity,” he said “They are strong, and they are prepared to take whatever action is necessary to secure an enterprise agreement that is acceptable to the workforce.” A BHP spokesperson said that with around 1200 people on site across its port facility, the company’s priority is continuing safe and productive operations.



“Vessels are continuing to be loaded with scheduled departures subject to usual port planning and tides,” the spokesperson said. “Our focus remains on reaching a fair and reasonable agreement. Our approach will deliver greater pay consistency across the workforce while locking in industry leading pay and conditions.” Beveridge said union members also remain committed to good faith negotiations when they next meet BHP on August 18. “But BHP must understand that the days of ignoring the legitimate claims of their workforce are over,” he said. “We are seeking an agreement that addresses the log of claims presented by employees at the beginning of this process.



“Our members know the impact of them withdrawing their labour at Port Hedland over this weekend was significant and BHP knows the impact of our members withdrawing their labour this weekend was significant. “Our hope is that this protected industrial action does exactly what it’s intended to do, which is sharpen all parties’ minds on finding a solution that works for everyone fast. “BHP must understand that the Combined Ports Unions will not be deterred by threats or intimidation.” An AWU spokesman said BHP management recently issued written communication threatening that any worker who participates in planned bans on ship loading activities would face the deduction of a full day’s pay, regardless of how many hours they worked on other essential tasks during their shift. However, a BHP spokesperson rejected those claims.



“Workplace laws are clear that we are not required to pay for the portion of an employee’s work that is subject to an industrial ban,” the BHP spokesperson said. “Unfortunately, with the additional 47 work activities the AWU advised us would be subject to their bans, there was no productive work left that the small number of employees who chose to take industrial action could undertake, and therefore no reason for them to attend work.” WA Industrial Relations Minister Simone McGurk urged both parties to continue to meet to “nut out the fine detail”. “If there’s a bit of give and take on both sides, I’m sure agreement could be reached,” she said.
